rubric: Face identity depends strongly on relationships among similar parts/configuration.
Face inversion often disproportionately impairs this processing.
Prosopagnosia can impair familiar face recognition despite some preserved other visual abilities.
Faces still share visual features/resources with objects, and expertise/task demands matter; a dissociation does not establish zero overlap.
commonMistakes: Configural processing does not mean faces have no features. Inversion and prosopagnosia support differentiated processing, but neither establishes zero overlap between face and object recognition or eliminates expertise-related alternatives.

questions.prompt: Compare strict early selection, late selection, and attenuation by selection stage and the fate of unattended input. Give an outcome that would challenge complete presemantic filtering, and explain why it would not uniquely prove late selection.
questions.explanation: Strict early selection filters on physical/channel properties before full semantic interpretation. Late selection allows meaning analysis before selection for response or awareness. Attenuation weakens rather than erases unattended input; unequal thresholds allow especially salient items to break through. A semantic effect from nominally unattended material, such as meaning-dependent interference or own-name detection, challenges complete exclusion before meaning analysis. Such an effect is compatible with later selection but can also reflect attenuation or a brief attention shift. A stronger test controls attention shifts and separates semantic processing from conscious report.
rubric: Strict early selection filters on physical/channel properties before full semantic interpretation.
Late selection allows meaning analysis before selection for response or awareness.
Attenuation weakens rather than erases unattended input; unequal thresholds allow especially salient items to break through.
A semantic effect from nominally unattended material, such as meaning-dependent interference or own-name detection, challenges complete exclusion before meaning analysis.

Such an effect is compatible with later selection but can also reflect attenuation or a brief attention shift. A stronger test controls attention shifts and separates semantic processing from conscious report.
commonMistakes: Name detection does not uniquely prove that every unattended word underwent full late selection. Attenuation with low thresholds or a brief attention shift can also produce meaningful breakthrough and require separate controls.

questions.prompt: In dichotic listening, people shadow one ear, detect physical changes in the other, but recall few unattended words. Occasionally their name breaks through. Explain evidence for early filtering and the challenge to a strict version.
questions.explanation: Shadowing concentrates processing on the selected channel. Preserved detection of voice/physical changes with poor word report supports physical-channel selection. Detection of a meaningful name challenges complete presemantic exclusion. Attenuation/threshold differences or occasional attention shifts must be distinguished experimentally; name detection alone does not prove full semantic processing of every unattended word.
rubric: Shadowing concentrates processing on the selected channel.
Preserved detection of voice/physical changes with poor word report supports physical-channel selection.
Detection of a meaningful name challenges complete presemantic exclusion.
Attenuation/threshold differences or occasional attention shifts must be distinguished experimentally; name detection alone does not prove full semantic processing of every unattended word.
commonMistakes: Poor later recall of unattended words is not proof of absolutely no processing, and noticing one's name is not proof of full conscious processing of every word. Distinguish physical-change detection, semantic influence, and report.

questions.prompt: Separate stimulus-driven and expectation-based priming in direction, effort, predictive-cue sensitivity, and costs to unexpected targets.
questions.explanation: Stimulus-driven priming reflects activation caused by input/recent related stimulation. Expectation-based priming reflects top-down preparation for predicted stimuli. In the course model, expectation-based preparation uses limited resources/effort and depends on cue predictiveness. Stimulus-driven facilitation is described as cost-free, whereas misallocated expectation can impair unexpected items relative to neutral baseline.
rubric: Stimulus-driven priming reflects activation caused by input/recent related stimulation.
Expectation-based priming reflects top-down preparation for predicted stimuli.
In the course model, expectation-based preparation uses limited resources/effort and depends on cue predictiveness.
Stimulus-driven facilitation is described as cost-free, whereas misallocated expectation can impair unexpected items relative to neutral baseline.
commonMistakes: Both forms can speed responses, so a benefit alone does not identify expectation. In the course account, cue predictiveness and costs to unexpected stimuli help distinguish resource-demanding preparation from cost-free stimulus-driven facilitation.

questions.prompt: Hypothetical mean RTs are: low-validity valid 470, neutral 500, invalid 500 ms; high-validity valid 420, neutral 500, invalid 550 ms. Compute valid benefits and invalid costs and interpret.
questions.explanation: Low-validity valid benefit is 500-470 = 30 ms. Low-validity invalid cost is 500-500 = 0 ms. High-validity benefit is 80 ms and invalid cost is 550-500 = 50 ms. Facilitation without cost fits stimulus-driven priming; added benefit plus invalid cost fits expectation-based allocation. Data are hypothetical, not the original lecture graph.
rubric: Low-validity valid benefit is 500-470 = 30 ms.
Low-validity invalid cost is 500-500 = 0 ms.
High-validity benefit is 80 ms and invalid cost is 550-500 = 50 ms.
Facilitation without cost fits stimulus-driven priming; added benefit plus invalid cost fits expectation-based allocation. Data are hypothetical, not the original lecture graph.
commonMistakes: Calculate each effect against its own neutral baseline: benefit is neutral minus valid, cost is invalid minus neutral. The 130 ms high-validity valid-invalid gap combines an 80 ms benefit and a 50 ms cost.

questions.prompt: Explain why a neutral-cue baseline matters in an attention experiment. Show why a valid-versus-invalid difference alone cannot distinguish benefits from costs.
questions.explanation: A neutral cue estimates performance without a directional expectation. Valid faster than neutral indicates benefit. Invalid slower than neutral indicates cost. A 60 ms valid-invalid gap could reflect benefit alone, cost alone, or both; compare both conditions to neutral and consider accuracy trade-offs.
rubric: A neutral cue estimates performance without a directional expectation.
Valid faster than neutral indicates benefit.
Invalid slower than neutral indicates cost.
A 60 ms valid-invalid gap could reflect benefit alone, cost alone, or both; compare both conditions to neutral and consider accuracy trade-offs.
commonMistakes: A valid-invalid difference is not automatically all a benefit or all a cost. Without neutral trials, the same gap can arise from faster valid responses, slower invalid responses, or both.

questions.prompt: Explain the spotlight analogy and two reasons it is incomplete. Include a Posner cueing result and an object-based result.
questions.explanation: Attention preferentially enhances processing at selected spatial locations, like a spotlight. Faster valid and slower invalid cue responses support spatial prioritization even with fixation. Attention can operate covertly and flexibly rather than being a literal beam with fixed borders. A same-object advantage at equal spatial distance shows selection follows object structure as well as coordinates.
rubric: Attention preferentially enhances processing at selected spatial locations, like a spotlight.
Faster valid and slower invalid cue responses support spatial prioritization even with fixation.
Attention can operate covertly and flexibly rather than being a literal beam with fixed borders.
A same-object advantage at equal spatial distance shows selection follows object structure as well as coordinates.
commonMistakes: The spotlight is an analogy, not a literal beam or a requirement to move the eyes. A same-object advantage at equal distance adds an object-based constraint without eliminating spatial attention.

questions.prompt: In a two-rectangle task, uncued targets are equally distant from the cue. RT is 330 ms on the same rectangle and 370 ms on the other. What is controlled and what inference follows? Give a limitation.
questions.explanation: Cue-target spatial distance is matched across those uncued conditions. Same-object targets are 40 ms faster. This supports object-based prioritization beyond a distance-only account. It does not show spatial attention is absent; stimulus geometry, eye position, and response demands must also be controlled.
rubric: Cue-target spatial distance is matched across those uncued conditions.
Same-object targets are 40 ms faster.
This supports object-based prioritization beyond a distance-only account.
It does not show spatial attention is absent; stimulus geometry, eye position, and response demands must also be controlled.
commonMistakes: Do not attribute the 40 ms same-object advantage simply to a shorter cue-target distance; that distance is matched. The result challenges a distance-only account but still permits spatial and object-based attention to coexist.

questions.prompt: Hypothetical RTs at set sizes 4, 8, 12 are 400, 410, 420 ms for feature search and 450, 550, 650 ms for conjunction search. Compute slopes, interpret, and predict an illusory-conjunction effect under divided attention.
questions.explanation: Feature slope is 20/8 = 2.5 ms/item. Conjunction slope is 200/8 = 25 ms/item. The larger conjunction cost fits attention-demanding feature binding/search in classic FIT. Reduced attention should increase incorrect feature combinations under brief exposure; slopes alone do not prove a strictly serial mechanism in all tasks.
rubric: Feature slope is 20/8 = 2.5 ms/item.
Conjunction slope is 200/8 = 25 ms/item.
The larger conjunction cost fits attention-demanding feature binding/search in classic FIT.
Reduced attention should increase incorrect feature combinations under brief exposure; slopes alone do not prove a strictly serial mechanism in all tasks.
commonMistakes: Divide change in RT by change in set size, not RT by total set size. The resulting 2.5 versus 25 ms/item slopes support the classic contrast but do not prove that every conjunction search uses an invariant serial process.

questions.prompt: A person misses left-side targets after right hemisphere injury. Another person binds colors to the wrong shapes during a brief dual task. Explain how each supports a role for attention without treating the deficits as identical.
questions.explanation: Neglect supports spatially organized attentional selection/representation. Its omissions are often contralesional and not merely primary blindness. Illusory conjunctions show feature detection can be preserved while binding fails. Together they motivate attentional roles in selecting locations/objects and binding features, but they are distinct behaviors/mechanisms.
rubric: Neglect supports spatially organized attentional selection/representation.
Its omissions are often contralesional and not merely primary blindness.
Illusory conjunctions show feature detection can be preserved while binding fails.
Together they motivate attentional roles in selecting locations/objects and binding features, but they are distinct behaviors/mechanisms.
commonMistakes: Neglect and illusory conjunctions are not the same error: one concerns which space is attended, the other which object receives a detected feature. Preserved features can coexist with either attentional problem.

questions.prompt: Distinguish task-general and task-specific resources. Give one kind of evidence for each and explain why a hybrid account can be needed.
questions.explanation: Task-specific resources are shared especially by tasks using similar modalities/codes. Greater interference for two verbal or two spatial tasks supports such pools. Cross-modal interference in response selection/executive control supports task-general limitations. A hybrid explains reduced overlap costs without assuming different modalities eliminate all competition.
rubric: Task-specific resources are shared especially by tasks using similar modalities/codes.
Greater interference for two verbal or two spatial tasks supports such pools.
Cross-modal interference in response selection/executive control supports task-general limitations.
A hybrid explains reduced overlap costs without assuming different modalities eliminate all competition.
commonMistakes: Different modalities do not guarantee no interference, and interference alone does not identify a single universal pool. Similarity effects support specific resources, while cross-modal response/control costs motivate a shared limitation.

questions.prompt: Predict relative dual-task interference for two difficult verbal tasks versus a well-practiced visual tracking task with a simple auditory task. State how similarity, difficulty, and practice affect your prediction.
questions.explanation: Similar verbal tasks compete more for overlapping specific resources. Greater difficulty increases demands and likely interference. Practice can reduce resource demands and improve coordination. The practiced cross-modal pair may interfere less but can still share response-selection/executive bottlenecks; actual task demands matter.
rubric: Similar verbal tasks compete more for overlapping specific resources.
Greater difficulty increases demands and likely interference.
Practice can reduce resource demands and improve coordination.
The practiced cross-modal pair may interfere less but can still share response-selection/executive bottlenecks; actual task demands matter.
commonMistakes: Practice does not guarantee zero interference. Similarity, difficulty, and overlapping response/control demands all matter; compare dual-task performance with each task's own single-task baseline.

questions.prompt: Compare automatic and controlled processes in attention demand, speed/flexibility, learning, and errors when goals change.
questions.explanation: Controlled processing is resource-demanding and goal-directed/flexible. Automatic processing is often fast and low-effort after extensive practice. Practice can shift performance toward automaticity but does not guarantee no resource use. Automatic habits can intrude after a rule change; controlled inhibition/switching may be needed, as in perseveration/Stroop-like conflict.
rubric: Controlled processing is resource-demanding and goal-directed/flexible.
Automatic processing is often fast and low-effort after extensive practice.
Practice can shift performance toward automaticity but does not guarantee no resource use.
Automatic habits can intrude after a rule change; controlled inhibition/switching may be needed, as in perseveration/Stroop-like conflict.
commonMistakes: Automatic is not synonymous with infallible or completely resource-free. A learned response can intrude when goals change, whereas controlled processing is more flexible but demands limited attention.

questions.prompt: Design a 2 x 2 dual-task study that can test task similarity and practice. Specify factors, outcome, prediction, and one control.
questions.explanation: Cross similar versus dissimilar secondary task with practiced versus unpracticed primary task. Measure dual-task costs relative to single-task baselines using RT and accuracy. Predict larger costs for similar/unpracticed combinations and reduced costs after practice. Match baseline difficulty or account for it, counterbalance order, and avoid interpreting a speed-accuracy trade-off as improvement. One suitable control suffices for the final point.
rubric: Cross similar versus dissimilar secondary task with practiced versus unpracticed primary task.
Measure dual-task costs relative to single-task baselines using RT and accuracy.
Predict larger costs for similar/unpracticed combinations and reduced costs after practice.
Match baseline difficulty or account for it, counterbalance order, and avoid interpreting a speed-accuracy trade-off as improvement. One suitable control suffices for the final point.
commonMistakes: Two conditions alone are not a full 2 x 2 design. Cross both similarity levels with both practice levels, and measure costs relative to single-task baselines so easier tasks or speed-accuracy trade-offs do not mimic a practice benefit.

questions.prompt: A student reads an unfamiliar word, compares possible meanings, and selects the meaning that fits the sentence. What makes these examples of mental processes?
choices: They involve operations on information, such as interpreting and comparing representations.
They are movements of the eyes, so their only relevant properties are muscular.
They count as mental processes only if the student can accurately describe every step.
They are names for brain structures rather than activities performed by a person.
questions.explanation: Mental processes are operations involved in acquiring, transforming, using, or responding to information. They need not all be consciously accessible.
choiceExplanations: Interpreting a word and comparing meanings describe information-processing operations, which are central objects of cognitive explanation.
Eye movements can provide evidence, but the interpretation and comparison of meanings are not explained by naming the muscles involved.
Many processing steps are not available to accurate introspection; conscious report is not a requirement for a mental process to exist.
A brain structure is a physical part of the nervous system; interpreting and comparing are activities that require an explanation of processing.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 1: meaning and examples of mental processes.

questions.prompt: Two trained observers give incompatible descriptions of the mental steps they used in the same task. Which limitation of introspection does this most directly illustrate?
choices: Private reports are useful only when every observer gives exactly the same description.
Private descriptions can be difficult to verify independently and may not accurately reveal processing.
Observable behavior is irrelevant whenever participants can report an experience.
Each report must be an accurate account of the mechanism because only the observer experienced it.
questions.explanation: Introspective descriptions can differ and are not direct, independently inspectable records of the operations that generated behavior.
choiceExplanations: Agreement can matter, but usefulness is not restricted to identical reports; the key issue is what evidence supports the reported processing account.
The researcher cannot directly inspect the reported private steps, so independent behavioral predictions help evaluate the competing descriptions.
Behavioral measures can test implications of the reports and provide evidence that does not depend solely on introspective access.
First-person access to an experience does not guarantee accurate access to all of the operations that produced that experience.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 1: introspection and the evidence used by competing approaches.

questions.prompt: Which project is primarily an artificial-intelligence goal, rather than a claim about how humans actually solve the task?
choices: Measuring how human recognition changes when objects are briefly presented.
Testing whether damage to a cortical region changes human recognition.
Building a program that reliably classifies objects, without requiring it to match human errors or processing.
Using people's response-time patterns to compare two accounts of recognition.
questions.explanation: An AI system can be designed to perform a task successfully without being a psychological model of the process used by people.
choiceExplanations: Manipulating viewing conditions and measuring human performance directly addresses the processes supporting human cognition.
Relating brain damage to human performance investigates the neural basis of cognition rather than merely engineering a successful classifier.
Successful machine performance is an engineering goal; a further argument and human-data comparisons are needed to treat it as a model of people.
Response-time predictions discriminate accounts of human processing, making this a cognitive-psychology question.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 1: cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and artificial intelligence.

questions.prompt: A researcher makes two tasks identical except that one requires comparing two remembered symbols. Responses take longer when comparison is required. Which explanation best uses the transcendental method?
choices: The researcher has directly seen the comparison happening inside the mind.
The extra time proves that only one brain region can compare symbols.
The slower responses establish that the participants were less motivated.
A comparison operation is a candidate explanation of the behavioral difference, to be tested against alternatives.
questions.explanation: The transcendental method works backward from observable outcomes to possible processes that could produce them; it does not directly observe those processes.
choiceExplanations: Response time is observable behavior; an internal comparison is inferred from it rather than directly seen by the researcher.
Behavioral timing alone does not localize the operation or establish that a single region is solely responsible for it.
Motivation could be an alternative explanation to control, but the timing difference does not by itself establish a motivational cause.
This proposes an internal operation to explain the observed difference while recognizing that other explanations still need to be evaluated.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 1: transcendental method and behavioral inference.

questions.prompt: A scientist has an exceptionally detailed map of the neurons active while someone solves a puzzle, but no account of what information is represented or how candidate solutions are evaluated. What remains missing?
choices: An explanation of the mental operations, which is not supplied by a list of active physical components alone.
Evidence that the brain has any role in thinking, because neural measurements never inform cognition.
Only the person's confidence rating; that rating uniquely identifies every processing step.
Nothing: the locations of active neurons automatically specify the algorithm used to solve the puzzle.
questions.explanation: Neural measurements can constrain cognitive explanations, but describing the physical implementation does not automatically specify representations and operations.
choiceExplanations: Knowing which components are active is valuable, yet one must still explain what information they process and how that processing solves the task.
Neural evidence is relevant and can constrain theories; the point is that it needs to be connected to an account of cognitive operations.
Confidence is another behavioral report, not a complete or uniquely reliable readout of the sequence of mental operations.
Different processing accounts can be compatible with a broad activity map; locations alone do not automatically reveal the algorithm.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 1: why studying the brain alone does not fully explain the mind.

questions.prompt: Two models predict the same percentage of correct responses, but only one predicts which similar symbols people systematically confuse. Why examine the errors?
choices: Errors are always random and therefore remove the need for an experiment.
The pattern of errors can constrain the representations or operations even when average accuracy cannot distinguish the models.
Any model that predicts an error must be a direct recording of conscious thought.
Errors identify an exact brain location without any neural measurements.
questions.explanation: A cognitive account should explain patterns in behavior, including systematic mistakes. Agreement on a single average does not mean the models are equivalent.
choiceExplanations: Systematic confusions are not merely random noise; their structure can distinguish explanations of the processing involved.
Different representations can produce different confusions, so error patterns provide an additional test beyond overall accuracy.
A successful behavioral prediction supports a model but does not turn the model into direct observation of private mental events.
Error patterns can constrain cognitive mechanisms, but anatomical localization requires additional kinds of evidence.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 1: using observable behavior to infer mental processes.

questions.prompt: A parallel-processing model and a serial-processing model both fit the mean response times from one experiment. Which next study would provide the most informative test between them?
choices: Repeat the same experiment with a larger sample, even if both models continue to predict the same distribution.
Ask participants which model sounds more like their experience, treating that report as decisive.
Manipulate the number of items under conditions where the models predict different response-time patterns, while measuring accuracy too.
Scan the brain during the original task and assume any active region uniquely identifies one of the models.
questions.explanation: A useful discriminating test targets a condition where the competing accounts predict different observations. Accuracy also matters when interpreting response-time differences.
choiceExplanations: A larger sample improves precision, but if the models predict the same observations it does not by itself discriminate their mechanisms.
Introspective reports can be data, but they do not directly reveal whether processing was serial or parallel and should not be treated as decisive.
This creates competing observable predictions and checks whether differences in speed are accompanied by different accuracy levels.
An activation map needs an explicit link to the competing computational accounts; a location is not automatically diagnostic of a mechanism.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 1: cognitive explanations, evidence, and the transcendental method.

questions.prompt: A computer and a person classify the same pictures equally accurately, but their error patterns differ greatly. What is the strongest conclusion about the program as a cognitive model?
choices: Equal accuracy is enough to establish the same mechanism because the correct classifications match.
The differing errors establish that no computational account could explain human recognition.
The error mismatch can be ignored as long as the program is more accurate on a second image set.
The program solves the task, but the mismatch counts against its adequacy as an account of the human processing that produced those errors.
questions.explanation: Engineering success and explanatory fit to human behavior are different standards. A cognitive model must address systematic human patterns, not only overall success.
choiceExplanations: Matching one summary measure leaves open different representations and operations, especially when the models make different mistakes.
A mismatch challenges this particular account, not the possibility of any computational explanation of human performance.
Greater machine accuracy could be valuable for engineering, but it does not explain why the human makes a different pattern of errors.
This recognizes useful task performance while treating human error patterns as relevant constraints on a psychological explanation.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 1: distinctions among cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and AI.

questions.prompt: On a cortical body map, the fingertips occupy much more cortex than their physical size would suggest. What principle does this illustrate?
choices: Cortical representation reflects functional demands and sensitivity rather than simply the body part's physical area.
The map is a physically scaled photograph of the body surface.
Large cortical representations occur only for the heaviest body parts.
Each body part receives exactly the same amount of cortex.
questions.explanation: Primary projection maps are systematically organized but distorted relative to body size. Behaviorally important, finely controlled or sensitive regions receive more representation.
choiceExplanations: A large fingertip representation reflects the functional demands of detailed sensory or motor processing rather than fingertip size alone.
The disproportionate fingertip representation directly contradicts a literal scale model of the body's physical dimensions.
Body mass does not determine the amount of cortex devoted to a body part; a light fingertip can have a substantial representation.
Equal cortical allocation would not produce the pronounced differences in representation emphasized by the cortical body map.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Exam 1 Review, primary projection areas; Study Guide, Module 2.

questions.prompt: The highlighted lobe contains primary auditory cortex. Which kind of information is most directly associated with that primary projection area?
choices: Commands for voluntary finger movements.
Basic properties of sounds, including pitch-related information.
The initial cortical map of positions in the visual field.
The body's temperature and hunger regulation.
questions.explanation: The temporal lobe contains primary auditory cortex. Its basic auditory representations should be distinguished from motor, visual, and hypothalamic functions.
choiceExplanations: Voluntary movement commands are associated with primary motor cortex in the frontal lobe, not primary auditory cortex.
Primary auditory cortex processes sound information; the review highlights organized representations related to pitch and volume.
The initial cortical visual map is associated with primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe rather than auditory cortex.
Homeostatic regulation such as temperature and hunger is broadly associated with the hypothalamus, not primary auditory cortex.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 2: lobes and primary projection areas; Exam 1 Review, primary projection maps.

questions.prompt: Which introductory description most appropriately distinguishes the thalamus from the hypothalamus?
choices: Thalamus: regulation of hunger and temperature; hypothalamus: the principal visual relay to cortex.
Thalamus: formation of new event memories; hypothalamus: analysis of sound in primary auditory cortex.
Thalamus: a major relay for sensory information; hypothalamus: regulation of internal bodily conditions.
Thalamus: emotional significance and threat learning; hypothalamus: skilled voluntary movement planning.
questions.explanation: The thalamus broadly relays and regulates information reaching cortex, while the hypothalamus contributes to homeostasis and related bodily regulation.
choiceExplanations: This reverses the broad distinction: homeostatic regulation is hypothalamic, while a major visual relay, the LGN, is thalamic.
New event-memory formation is associated with the hippocampus; primary auditory cortex is cortical and is not the hypothalamus.
This captures the course-level contrast between a major sensory relay and a regulator of internal bodily needs and conditions.
Emotional significance is a broad amygdala function, while purposeful movement planning involves cortical systems; this pairing misassigns both.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 2: broad functions of the four introductory limbic/subcortical structures.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the amygdala's broad role without treating it as a single-purpose 'fear button'?
choices: It provides the principal thalamic relay for visual input to cortex.
It regulates internal bodily needs such as hunger and temperature.
It is chiefly responsible for forming new memories of event relationships.
It contributes to evaluating emotionally significant information and emotional learning.
questions.explanation: The amygdala contributes to processing emotional significance, including threat-related learning, but its role should not be reduced to one emotion or an exclusive mechanism.
choiceExplanations: The LGN in the thalamus is a major visual relay; that description does not identify the broad function of the amygdala.
Homeostatic regulation is broadly associated with the hypothalamus, which should be distinguished from the amygdala.
Formation of new event memories is a broad hippocampal role; the amygdala is especially associated with emotional significance and learning.
This states a broad emotional-processing role while avoiding an unsupported claim that only fear or only one region is involved.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 2: broad limbic/subcortical functions.

questions.prompt: Which task places the clearest demand on the hippocampus's broad introductory function?
choices: Forming a memory of the new people and events encountered at today's lab meeting.
Adjusting body temperature after standing in a hot room.
Generating the initial cortical response to the pitch of a tone.
Relaying retinal signals through the LGN toward visual cortex.
questions.explanation: The hippocampus is especially important for forming new memories of events and their relationships. This is distinct from homeostasis and early sensory processing.
choiceExplanations: Remembering a newly encountered event and its participants fits the hippocampus's broad role in forming new event memories.
Regulation of internal conditions such as temperature is broadly associated with the hypothalamus rather than the hippocampus.
Basic cortical sound processing is associated with auditory cortex in the temporal lobe; a whole lobe and one subcortical structure are not interchangeable.
The LGN is a thalamic visual relay in the pathway to V1, not a function performed by the hippocampus.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 2: broad functions of limbic/subcortical structures.

questions.prompt: The highlighted lobe includes primary somatosensory cortex. Which observation would most directly test the function of that primary area?
choices: Whether a person can explain the plot of a remembered film.
Whether touching different locations on the opposite hand produces distinguishable sensations.
Whether a person can recognize a familiar melody by its title.
Whether hunger changes after a meal.
questions.explanation: Primary somatosensory cortex represents bodily sensory input, largely from the opposite side. A controlled touch-location task directly probes that mapping.
choiceExplanations: Explaining a film involves memory and language; it is not a direct test of the primary cortical representation of body sensation.
Discriminating touch locations probes a bodily sensory map and its largely contralateral organization in somatosensory cortex.
Naming a melody involves auditory recognition and other processing rather than directly testing the primary body-sensation map.
Changes in hunger concern regulation of bodily needs, which is broadly linked to the hypothalamus rather than this primary cortical area.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 2: lobe functions, primary projection areas, and contralateral organization.

questions.prompt: In a hypothetical case, a person recognizes a comb, understands the command to demonstrate its use, and can move their arm with normal strength, but cannot organize the familiar action. Which association-cortex problem best fits?
choices: Complete loss of visual sensation.
Loss of temperature regulation.
Apraxia: difficulty carrying out learned, purposeful actions despite sufficient basic movement capacity.
Aphasia: a deficit defined specifically by reduced muscle strength.
questions.explanation: Apraxia concerns the organization or execution of learned purposeful actions and should be distinguished from a simple inability to generate muscle force.
choiceExplanations: The defining observation concerns organizing an action despite preserved strength; no complete loss of visual sensation is described.
Temperature regulation is a homeostatic function and does not explain the selective difficulty organizing a familiar purposeful movement.
This fits a problem in learned-action organization while acknowledging the preserved basic motor capacity specified in the scenario.
Aphasia concerns language impairment, and neither aphasia nor the described problem is defined simply as a reduction in muscle strength.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Exam 1 Review, association areas and apraxia; Study Guide, Module 2.

questions.prompt: A person hears a spoken instruction and can detect its volume, but has acquired difficulty understanding its words and producing meaningful sentences. Which broad syndrome is most relevant?
choices: Hemispatial neglect, because all failures of understanding are failures to attend to one side.
Apraxia, because any learned task is a movement-sequencing deficit.
Loss of all primary auditory input, despite the preserved sound detection.
Aphasia, because the difficulty concerns language processing rather than just detecting sound.
questions.explanation: Aphasia is an acquired language impairment. Preserved basic sound detection does not ensure intact comprehension or production of language.
choiceExplanations: Neglect involves a spatial bias in attention, not every failure to understand information; no one-sided spatial deficit is described here.
Apraxia concerns purposeful action organization, whereas this description specifically emphasizes understanding and producing language.
The person still detects sound and its volume, so a complete loss of auditory input does not fit the stated pattern.
The selective language difficulty is consistent with aphasia; basic sensory detection and higher-level language processing can be distinguished.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Exam 1 Review, association areas and aphasia; Study Guide, Module 2.

questions.prompt: The highlighted lobe includes prefrontal association cortex. A person can execute individual movements but repeatedly acts before considering the task goal. Which broad function is most relevant?
choices: Planning and inhibition of inappropriate responses.
Converting incoming photons into retinal signals.
Detecting the pitch of a tone in primary auditory cortex.
Regulating hunger through the hypothalamus.
questions.explanation: Prefrontal association systems contribute to planning, strategic behavior, and inhibition. Those functions differ from the capacity to execute individual movements.
choiceExplanations: Considering goals and withholding premature actions directly fit the broad planning and inhibition functions emphasized for prefrontal cortex.
Photons are transduced by retinal photoreceptors, not by prefrontal cortex; the scenario does not describe a failure to see the task.
Primary auditory processing is associated with temporal cortex and does not directly explain acting without considering a goal.
Hypothalamic regulation of bodily needs is distinct from the described failure of planning and response inhibition.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Exam 1 Review, association cortex and prefrontal damage; Study Guide, Module 2.

questions.prompt: A carefully localized disruption affects the right primary somatosensory representation of the hand. Which outcome best follows from the course's contralateral organization principle?
choices: A selective loss of hearing in both ears is the most direct prediction.
Disrupted sensation from the left hand is a stronger initial prediction than disrupted sensation from the right hand.
All functions of the entire left side of the body must permanently disappear.
The right hand must be affected because 'right cortex' means 'right body.'
questions.explanation: Contralateral organization predicts that the right primary somatosensory hand representation chiefly concerns sensation from the left hand, without implying total bodily loss.
choiceExplanations: The manipulated site is a hand-related somatosensory representation, not primary auditory cortex, so this is not the direct prediction.
The opposite-side mapping makes left-hand sensation the relevant initial prediction for a right cortical somatosensory disruption.
A localized sensory disruption does not establish loss of every motor and sensory function across an entire body side, or permanence.
Contralateral means opposite-sided; this answer instead describes an ipsilateral relationship and reverses the relevant principle.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 2: primary projection areas and contralateral organization.

questions.prompt: In two hypothetical cases of temporal-lobe injury, one person detects sounds but struggles to identify familiar spoken words; another identifies words but struggles to form memories of new events. Which inference is best justified?
choices: Temporal-lobe damage has no interpretable relation to behavior because the two patients differ.
One of the cases must involve another lobe because a lobe can support only one cognitive function.
The broad lobe contains different systems, and preserved versus impaired abilities constrain the account more than the lobe label alone.
The behavioral difference uniquely identifies the exact damaged structure in each patient without imaging or further testing.
questions.explanation: Broad lobe labels encompass multiple areas and functions. Different selective impairments motivate more detailed hypotheses but do not uniquely locate individual lesions.
choiceExplanations: Differences across cases can be informative about functional organization; they do not make all anatomical-behavioral relationships uninterpretable.
A lobe can include systems for hearing, recognition, language, and memory; a different deficit does not require a different lobe.
This uses the selective patterns to refine a coarse anatomical label while preserving uncertainty about exact structures and mechanisms.
The patterns suggest hypotheses, but performance alone is insufficient to uniquely establish the precise anatomical extent of either lesion.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 2: broad lobe functions and association versus primary projection areas.

questions.prompt: One hypothetical patient detects a light and its location but cannot identify the pictured tool. Another fails to detect the light in the tested region. What is the most defensible comparison?
choices: Both deficits must occur at the same processing stage because both tests use visual stimuli.
The recognition deficit must reflect complete loss of retinal input, despite preserved light detection.
The first pattern uniquely proves damage to one named association area, while the second uniquely proves a V1 lesion.
The patterns distinguish recognition from more basic visual detection, but neither pattern alone uniquely locates its anatomical cause.
questions.explanation: Preserved abilities help distinguish levels of visual processing. The distinction is meaningful without claiming that a behavioral pattern identifies one unique lesion site.
choiceExplanations: Sharing a sensory modality does not make detection and recognition the same operation; their different preservation is the key evidence.
Complete retinal-input loss does not fit preserved detection and localization of the light in the tested conditions.
Both patterns admit more than one anatomical cause, so these exact locations require additional anatomical and behavioral evidence.
This distinguishes the affected functions while keeping the strength of anatomical inference within what the observations establish.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 2: primary projection and association areas; Exam 1 Review, agnosia.

questions.prompt: A primary projection map is orderly, but sensitive fingertips have more representation than a much larger skin surface. Which statement reconciles both observations?
choices: Mapping preserves systematic relationships without requiring cortical area to scale directly with physical body area.
Orderly mapping requires each square centimeter of skin to occupy the same amount of cortex.
The disproportionate map makes it impossible to predict any body-location relationship from cortical location.
The large fingertip representation establishes that this primary map alone explains skilled use of tools.
questions.explanation: A map can be topographically organized and still magnify functionally important regions. Basic representation does not itself explain every higher-level use of that information.
choiceExplanations: This distinguishes systematic spatial organization from literal geometric scaling, allowing cortical magnification of sensitive body regions.
Equal scaling is contradicted by the disproportionate representation; orderly does not mean an undistorted physical replica.
Distortion in scale does not eliminate organization, so neighboring or distinct body locations can still have systematic cortical representations.
Primary mapping contributes to sensation or movement, but learned purposeful tool use also requires further organization and association-level processing.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Exam 1 Review, primary projection and association areas; Study Guide, Module 2.

questions.prompt: For a typical neuron in the course's introductory diagram, which pairing correctly distinguishes receiving input from sending chemical output?
choices: Dendrites carry the outgoing spike to distant targets; axon terminals integrate most incoming signals.
Dendrites commonly receive synaptic input; axon terminals release transmitter onto target cells.
The cell body releases transmitter directly into every target synapse; the axon only receives input.
Myelin detects incoming transmitter; the synaptic cleft generates the outgoing action potential.
questions.explanation: The introductory neuron model distinguishes dendritic input, integration near the cell body and axon origin, axonal conduction, and transmitter release from terminals.
choiceExplanations: This reverses the typical introductory organization: dendrites commonly receive input and the axon carries output toward its terminals.
This matches the typical input-output arrangement: synaptic input onto dendrites and output from terminals contacting another cell.
The soma contributes to integration and cell maintenance, while the axon conducts output toward terminals rather than functioning only as an input structure.
Myelin insulates axons rather than serving as the postsynaptic receptor, and the cleft is a gap rather than a site of spike generation.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 3: neuron parts and their functions.

questions.prompt: Which description of myelin best fits its role in the neuron's communication process?
choices: It binds transmitter on the postsynaptic membrane and determines the sign of that receptor response.
It packages transmitter at the axon terminal for release into the synaptic cleft.
It insulates portions of an axon and supports efficient, rapid signal conduction.
It combines graded incoming signals at the cell body before threshold is reached.
questions.explanation: Myelin is an insulating covering around portions of an axon. It assists conduction along the axon rather than acting as the chemical messenger between cells.
choiceExplanations: This describes a receptor-related role in chemical signaling, whereas myelin is an insulating covering associated with axons.
Transmitter packaging and release involve the presynaptic terminal and vesicles, not the insulating myelin around axonal segments.
Insulation supports rapid propagation along myelinated axons, distinguishing myelin from the transmitter and the receiving receptor.
Integration of incoming effects is a neuron-level process involving dendrites, soma, and spike initiation; it is not the defining function of myelin.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 3: neuron parts and neural communication.

questions.prompt: At a chemical synapse from neuron A to neuron B, what do 'presynaptic' and 'postsynaptic' identify?
choices: A is the excitatory cell and B is the inhibitory cell at this connection.
A is the cell body and B is the axon of a single neuron.
A is the receptor-bearing receiving side and B releases the transmitter.
A is the transmitter-releasing side of this connection; B is the receiving side.
questions.explanation: Presynaptic and postsynaptic describe the two sides of a particular synaptic connection, not a neuron's hemisphere or a fixed excitatory versus inhibitory identity.
choiceExplanations: Presynaptic and postsynaptic indicate direction of transmission at a connection, not a fixed excitatory or inhibitory identity of each cell.
The scenario describes a connection between two neurons, not two named parts of the same neuron.
This reverses the direction specified by a synapse from A to B: A is the presynaptic sender and B the postsynaptic receiver.
This correctly describes their relationship at this synapse; a neuron can receive at one connection and send at another.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 3: how neurons communicate across chemical synapses.

questions.prompt: An inhibitory input arrives while a neuron is receiving excitatory inputs. Which definition of inhibition is most appropriate?
choices: It tends to reduce the likelihood that the receiving neuron will produce an action potential.
It guarantees that no action potential occurs, irrespective of simultaneous excitation.
It reduces the amplitude of each action potential that the receiving neuron generates.
It means the presynaptic cell has stopped communicating with the receiving cell.
questions.explanation: Inhibition is an active synaptic influence that makes firing less likely under the relevant conditions; it is not necessarily an absolute veto or a lack of signaling.
choiceExplanations: The functional distinction concerns firing probability: inhibition opposes or limits excitation's tendency to bring the neuron to threshold.
The integrated input pattern matters; an inhibitory influence can be outweighed and need not act as an unconditional veto.
Inhibition influences whether a spike is generated, rather than making an otherwise generated all-or-none action potential proportionally smaller.
Inhibitory transmission is an active influence on the receiving cell, so absence of excitation does not imply absence of communication.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 3: excitation versus inhibition.

questions.prompt: In a hypothetical experiment, an action potential reaches neuron A's terminal normally, but transmitter release from that terminal is blocked. What is the most direct prediction for its chemical synapse onto neuron B?
choices: The action potential must grow taller to jump across the gap.
The usual transmitter-dependent response in B will be reduced or absent even though A conducted a spike.
B must fire normally because all neural communication is purely electrical.
The block proves that B has no functioning receptors anywhere on its surface.
questions.explanation: Electrical propagation to a terminal is not sufficient for ordinary chemical transmission if the transmitter is not released to act on the receiving cell.
choiceExplanations: At the chemical synapse described, transmission depends on released messenger rather than a larger electrical spike leaping across the cleft.
The manipulation separates intact presynaptic conduction from failed chemical output, so this synapse's normal effect on B is interrupted.
Chemical signaling across the synapse is an essential part of the electrochemical sequence and cannot be omitted from the prediction.
A release blockade concerns neuron A's output; it does not establish any defect in B's receptors or its other synaptic inputs.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 3: electrochemical signaling and the sequence of neuronal communication.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical drug prevents a particular transmitter from binding to its postsynaptic receptor, but does not change its release. Which observation is most expected at that receptor-mediated connection?
choices: The transmitter can no longer exist anywhere in the presynaptic neuron.
The presynaptic axon must become the postsynaptic dendrite.
The transmitter can be present in the cleft while its usual effect through the blocked receptor is diminished.
Every other synapse in the brain must become inhibitory.
questions.explanation: Transmitter availability and receptor activation are separate steps. Blocking the relevant receptor can prevent an effect despite normal release.
choiceExplanations: The manipulation blocks binding rather than synthesis or release; it does not imply the transmitter has disappeared from the sending cell.
Blocking a receptor changes signaling through that receptor, not the anatomical identity of the connected axon and dendrite.
The messenger still reaches the cleft, but it cannot produce its ordinary receptor-dependent effect when the relevant binding is blocked.
A local receptor-specific manipulation does not determine the sign or function of every other synapse in the brain.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 3: chemical synaptic signaling and what determines a signal's effect.

questions.prompt: In a simplified demonstration, a neuron fires after three excitatory inputs arrive close together, but not when the same inputs are widely separated. What best explains the difference?
choices: Three inputs always create an action potential three times taller than a normal one.
Separated inputs must use a different neurotransmitter, even though none was changed.
A neuron receives only one synapse, so the described result is impossible.
Nearby-in-time postsynaptic effects can combine to reach threshold; separated effects may decay before they combine sufficiently.
questions.explanation: The timing of graded inputs affects their summation and whether threshold is reached. This is distinct from increasing the amplitude of individual action potentials.
choiceExplanations: Inputs can combine before threshold, but the generated action potential is not a proportionally taller sum of the incoming signals.
The observation changes input timing, so an unmeasured transmitter change is unnecessary and unsupported as an explanation.
Neurons commonly receive multiple inputs, and integrating their effects is a central part of the course's communication account.
This explains the timing dependence through summation and decay of graded effects rather than changing the size of the resulting spike.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 3: detailed neuronal communication, excitation, and integration of inputs.

questions.prompt: A signal travels along a neuron's axon, then influences another neuron through released transmitter. Which description keeps the two communication stages distinct?
choices: Changes in membrane voltage propagate along the axon; a chemical messenger acts on receptors across the synapse.
Transmitter molecules themselves travel down the axon as the action potential and become electrical charges in the next cell.
The synaptic cleft is a continuous part of the first neuron's membrane, so the same spike passes through unchanged.
Electrical activity occurs only in muscles; both stages between neurons are entirely chemical.
questions.explanation: Neural communication is electrochemical because voltage changes propagate within the neuron and chemical messengers commonly mediate transmission between neurons.
choiceExplanations: This identifies the electrical event along the axonal membrane and the chemical receptor-mediated event at the synapse.
An action potential is a propagating voltage change, not a packet of transmitter molecules turning into electrical charge in the next neuron.
A chemical synapse contains a gap between separate membranes; the presynaptic action potential does not simply continue through one unbroken membrane.
Neurons themselves produce electrical changes in membrane voltage; those changes are not restricted to muscles.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 3: why neural communication is electrochemical.

questions.prompt: In a simplified threshold model, a neuron fires when the net graded input reaches +5 units. Two simultaneous excitatory inputs contribute +4 and +3; an inhibitory input contributes -3. In a second trial only inhibition changes to -1. What does the model predict?
choices: Both trials produce spikes because each contains two excitatory inputs and only one inhibitory input.
Only the second trial reaches threshold; the change alters whether a spike occurs, not its amplitude.
Neither trial produces a spike because any inhibitory input prevents firing regardless of other input.
Both trials produce spikes, with the second spike taller in proportion to the larger net input.
questions.explanation: In this explicitly simplified model the net inputs are +4 and +6. Only +6 reaches the +5 threshold; action-potential amplitude does not represent that graded sum.
choiceExplanations: The contributions must be integrated by their effects, not merely by counting the number of excitatory versus inhibitory inputs.
The first total is +4 and the second is +6, so only the second meets the threshold; graded input size is distinct from all-or-none spike amplitude.
An inhibitory input reduces the net excitation, but sufficiently strong combined excitation can still bring the neuron to threshold.
The first trial stays below threshold, and the second does not generate a proportionally taller spike simply because its net input is larger.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 3: excitation, inhibition, and detailed neural communication.

questions.prompt: A researcher sees a presynaptic spike but no postsynaptic action potential. Why is it premature to conclude that this synapse transmitted nothing?
choices: Every postsynaptic effect is itself an action potential, so the conclusion is already certain.
A presynaptic spike proves the next neuron fired, regardless of the recording.
The synapse may have produced an inhibitory or subthreshold excitatory effect without triggering a postsynaptic spike.
Chemical transmission cannot influence electrical activity, so the two observations are unrelated.
questions.explanation: Synaptic communication need not produce an immediate action potential in the receiving neuron. Graded excitatory or inhibitory effects can occur without threshold crossing.
choiceExplanations: Postsynaptic potentials are not all-or-none action potentials; a change can occur without producing an outgoing spike.
A presynaptic spike does not guarantee a postsynaptic spike, because release, receptor effects, and integration intervene.
This recognizes meaningful synaptic effects that change the receiving neuron's state without necessarily causing it to fire.
Chemical receptor activation can change postsynaptic electrical conditions; the link between those stages is central to electrochemical signaling.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 3: synaptic effects, excitation, inhibition, and neural communication.

questions.prompt: A researcher asks whether two responses occurred 30 milliseconds apart or at the same time. Which measurement property matters most for that question?
choices: Spatial resolution: the ability to distinguish two nearby anatomical locations.
Functional selectivity: whether a region responds more to one category than another.
Causal control: whether the researcher experimentally disrupts a candidate region.
Temporal resolution: the ability to distinguish events close together in time.
questions.explanation: The question concerns the timing of events, so temporal resolution is central. A visually detailed spatial map does not necessarily resolve rapid timing differences.
choiceExplanations: Fine spatial resolution concerns where signals arise, rather than whether their times differ by a few milliseconds.
A selective response can help characterize function, but selectivity does not by itself provide the required precision in event timing.
An intervention can address causal contribution, but the stated question specifically requires resolving when measured responses occur.
Fine temporal resolution directly addresses whether two measured events can be distinguished in time at the relevant scale.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 4: temporal resolution and appropriate neuroimaging questions.

questions.prompt: What is the most useful introductory distinction between structural MRI and fMRI?
choices: Structural MRI depicts anatomy; fMRI measures an indirect blood-oxygenation-related signal associated with activity.
Structural MRI records scalp electrical potentials; fMRI directly counts action potentials in each neuron.
Structural MRI temporarily disrupts a cortical site; fMRI tests performance after that disruption.
Structural MRI and fMRI both measure anatomy only, with no activity-related contrast available.
questions.explanation: Structural MRI and functional MRI answer different questions: anatomical structure versus activity-related hemodynamic changes. Neither is a direct recording of thoughts.
choiceExplanations: This separates anatomical imaging from the indirect functional signal used to compare activity across tasks or conditions.
Scalp electrical recording describes EEG; fMRI measures a hemodynamic signal rather than directly counting individual spikes.
Temporary cortical interference is associated with TMS in this comparison; structural MRI is an imaging method, not that intervention.
Structural anatomy is central to structural MRI, but fMRI uses activity-related signal changes to compare conditions.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 4: neuroimaging methods and their uses.

questions.prompt: What does good spatial resolution make it easier for a neuroimaging method to distinguish?
choices: Two mental operations occurring at exactly the same location but a millisecond apart.
Signals associated with nearby anatomical locations rather than blending them into one broad location.
Causal necessity from correlation without any additional evidence.
A participant's intended strategy from every other possible strategy automatically.
questions.explanation: Spatial resolution concerns location. It does not by itself solve temporal ordering, reverse inference, or the difference between correlation and causation.
choiceExplanations: Distinguishing rapidly separated events is a temporal-resolution problem, even if the events happen at the same anatomical site.
Finer localization helps separate nearby sources or structures, which is the central meaning of spatial resolution.
Precisely locating a correlated signal does not establish that the region is necessary for the behavior being measured.
Knowing where a signal occurs does not uniquely identify which strategy or mental process generated it.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 4: spatial resolution and limits of localization.

questions.prompt: In a hypothetical task, a region becomes more active when people prepare a response. A student concludes that the region must cause the response. How does the review's speedometer analogy challenge that conclusion?
choices: It shows that brain measurements can never be reliable.
It proves that the region has no role in preparing a response.
A signal can reliably accompany an event without being the mechanism that produces it.
It shows that any highly active region is necessarily the only causal region.
questions.explanation: A speedometer reading tracks speed but is not what accelerates the car. Likewise, activity accompanying a task does not alone establish causal necessity.
choiceExplanations: The analogy concerns interpretation of reliable covariation, not a claim that measurement is inherently unreliable.
Lack of proof of necessity is not proof of irrelevance; the region may participate, but a stronger causal claim needs more evidence.
This captures the analogy: correlation can be informative without identifying the component that causes or is necessary for the outcome.
High activity is not an exclusivity or necessity test, and multiple systems can contribute to preparing and executing a response.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Exam 1 Review, reverse inference and speedometer analogy; Study Guide, Module 4.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical experiment asks whether a visual response precedes a later decision-related response by a small fraction of a second. Which design is best matched to this timing question?
choices: A structural MRI alone, because an anatomical image directly orders mental events.
An fMRI activation map interpreted as a millisecond-by-millisecond recording of spikes.
A verbal report after the experiment treated as an exact time series of neural processing.
An EEG/ERP design that measures stimulus-locked electrical responses over time, while acknowledging localization limits.
questions.explanation: EEG and event-related potentials offer fine temporal information, making them useful for timing questions, though they do not provide equally precise source localization.
choiceExplanations: Structural anatomy alone does not provide the time course of task-related electrical responses or the ordering of processing events.
The fMRI signal is indirect and temporally sluggish relative to neuronal spikes, so that interpretation exceeds its timing resolution.
Retrospective experience reports do not supply a precise millisecond record of the underlying neural events.
This uses the strength of EEG/ERP for timing while retaining the distinction between temporal sensitivity and anatomical localization.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 4: best temporal resolution and appropriate research questions.

questions.prompt: In hypothetical data, area R responds strongly during attention, memory, and movement tasks. During a new task, R is active. Why is 'the person must be remembering' a weak inference?
choices: R's activity is not selective to remembering, so several different processes could explain it.
Any region that supports more than one task cannot ever show measurable activity.
The observation proves that the person is definitely not remembering.
More detailed images would automatically make the region exclusive to memory.
questions.explanation: Reverse inference is weak when the observed activity occurs in many processes. Knowing that memory can activate a region does not make activation uniquely diagnostic of memory.
choiceExplanations: The known range of tasks associated with R supplies alternative explanations, undermining a unique inference from activity to remembering.
Multifunctional participation is compatible with measurable activity; it is a limitation on interpretation, not on detecting signals.
A weak claim of certainty does not imply the opposite is certain; memory remains one possible contributor among others.
Better spatial detail does not by itself change the functional selectivity of a region or remove alternative explanations.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 4: reverse inference problem.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical TMS study finds slower responses after stimulation, but the comparison condition has no click, scalp sensation, or distraction. What is the most important limitation?
choices: Response times can never be used to study cognition.
The slowing might reflect nonspecific stimulation effects, so matched comparison conditions are needed before attributing it to the targeted computation.
The finding proves that the stimulated region performs every mental operation.
TMS becomes purely observational whenever a participant makes a button press.
questions.explanation: Manipulation supports causal reasoning only with appropriate controls. Sensation, sound, and distraction can offer alternatives to disruption of the hypothesized local computation.
choiceExplanations: Response time is a useful behavioral measure; the problem is the interpretation of an inadequately controlled manipulation.
Controls that address stimulation-related sensations and nonspecific effects help isolate the consequence of disrupting the intended system.
A slower response in one task cannot establish that a region implements every process, especially with uncontrolled alternative causes.
TMS remains an intervention; the response method does not remove that fact, although the intervention still requires careful control.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 4: methods for causal evidence and their interpretation.

questions.prompt: In hypothetical data, controls score 90% on naming and 70% on matching. Patient A scores 85% and 35%, respectively. Which additional pattern would most strengthen a double-dissociation argument rather than a general task-difficulty account?
choices: Patient B scores 88% on naming and 38% on matching.
Patient B scores 45% on naming and 35% on matching.
Patient B scores 40% on naming and 68% on matching, with comparable sensory and response requirements controlled.
Patient B scores 90% on naming and 70% on matching.
questions.explanation: Patient A has relatively preserved naming and impaired matching against the control baseline. Selectively impaired naming with near-control matching supplies the complementary pattern.
choiceExplanations: This largely repeats the first selective pattern; repeating a deficit strengthens its reliability but does not provide the opposite selective impairment.
Both tasks are substantially impaired relative to controls, which does not clearly demonstrate selectively preserved matching in the second case.
This reverses the relative impairment: naming is affected while matching is near its control baseline, strengthening the argument for partial functional separation.
Normal performance provides a useful comparison but does not demonstrate the complementary selective deficit needed for a double dissociation.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 4: double dissociation; Exam 1 Review, localization of function.

questions.prompt: Suppose an accessible cortical region shows an fMRI preference for faces over houses. In a hypothetical TMS follow-up, which result most strengthens a task-specific causal claim, assuming baseline task difficulty and sensory effects of stimulation are controlled?
choices: Faces evoke stronger fMRI activity again in a second group, without any intervention.
Both judgments become equally slower after stimulation at either the target site or a control site.
Face judgments are slower than house judgments even before any stimulation is applied.
Target-site stimulation selectively impairs face judgments relative to sham and control-site stimulation, while house judgments remain comparatively preserved.
questions.explanation: Selective behavioral impairment after a controlled intervention is stronger causal evidence than repeated preference alone. Controls help separate targeted disruption from baseline and nonspecific effects.
choiceExplanations: Replication strengthens evidence for a reliable response preference, but remains correlational rather than testing the behavioral consequence of disruption.
Equal slowing across tasks and sites fits nonspecific interference better than a selective contribution of the targeted site to face judgments.
A preexisting difficulty difference does not show that disrupting the candidate region changes processing; intervention-relative comparisons are required.
This supplies an intervention-related selective effect with relevant comparisons, supporting a contribution under the tested conditions without proving exclusivity.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Exam 1 Review, FFA versus PPA and localization; Study Guide, Module 4.

questions.prompt: A region is active during a task, but a controlled TMS test at one time produces no detectable performance change. Which interpretation properly limits both the imaging and intervention findings?
choices: The activity shows task association; this particular intervention did not demonstrate a necessary contribution, but does not rule out a contribution at other times or conditions.
The null TMS result shows that the region can never contribute to the task, regardless of timing or the effectiveness of stimulation.
The activation establishes necessity, so the null intervention result need not influence the account.
The two findings cancel each other, leaving no evidence even that activity was associated with the task.
questions.explanation: Association and intervention effects answer different questions. A null effect is bounded by timing, intervention effectiveness, task conditions, and measurement sensitivity.
choiceExplanations: This preserves the positive association while stating the actual scope of the negative intervention result and avoiding an unlimited conclusion of irrelevance.
One null result does not establish successful disruption at every relevant time or rule out all possible contributions of the region.
Activation alone does not establish necessity, so it cannot justify disregarding the additional intervention evidence.
A null behavioral effect does not erase the observed task-activity association; the observations constrain different kinds of claims.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 4: causal evidence, localization, and limitations of methods.

questions.prompt: A recording is made from an axon as it leaves the eye within the optic nerve. Which cell type supplies that axon?
choices: A rod or cone photoreceptor.
A retinal ganglion cell.
A retinal bipolar cell.
An LGN relay cell.
questions.explanation: Retinal ganglion-cell axons gather to form the optic nerve. Rods and cones detect light, and bipolar cells pass signals within the retina before ganglion-cell output.
choiceExplanations: Rods and cones initiate visual signaling by detecting photons, but their processes do not form the optic nerve leaving the eye.
The review identifies ganglion-cell axons as the fibers that leave the eye together in the optic nerve and project toward the LGN.
Bipolar cells relay signals between photoreceptors and ganglion cells within the retina rather than supplying the optic nerve axons.
LGN cells are in the thalamic relay and send output onward toward cortex; they are not retinal cells whose axons leave the eye.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Exam 1 Review, the retina; Study Guide, Module 5: retina-to-cortex information flow.

questions.prompt: Which description belongs in an account of a visual neuron's receptive field?
choices: Only the neuron's anatomical location inside the skull.
Only the part of the retina on which the neuron is physically located.
The region of visual space and stimulus conditions that affect the neuron's response.
The participant's entire conscious visual experience on a trial.
questions.explanation: A receptive field is specified in relation to visual input that influences a neuron's response. It is not simply the physical position of that neuron in the nervous system.
choiceExplanations: Anatomical location describes where the neuron is, whereas a receptive field describes which visual input affects its activity.
Cortical neurons also have receptive fields even though they are not physically in the retina, so retinal location alone is not the definition.
This matches the review's definition in terms of a region of the visual field and the type of stimulus to which the neuron responds.
One neuron's receptive field is not identical to the whole conscious scene, which depends on processing across many neurons.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Exam 1 Review, receptive fields; Study Guide, Module 5.

questions.prompt: A researcher plots a V1 neuron's response rate against the orientation of a bar held at one location. What would a broad tuning curve imply?
choices: The neuron has no receptive field anywhere in visual space.
The neuron must respond equally to every orientation because tuning permits only one response level.
The graph specifies the exact location of the neuron within the occipital lobe.
The neuron can respond to a range of orientations, with some producing stronger responses than others.
questions.explanation: Tuning describes how response strength varies with a stimulus property. A preferred orientation need not be the only orientation that evokes activity.
choiceExplanations: A neuron can have both a spatial receptive field and broad orientation tuning; the two measurements describe different aspects of responsiveness.
Tuning curves depict graded differences in response across a stimulus dimension rather than requiring an identical response to all values.
An orientation-response plot measures functional selectivity, not the neuron's anatomical coordinates inside cortex.
A broad curve indicates responsiveness across several values of the feature, typically with a maximum near a preferred orientation.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 5: tuning curves and V1; Exam 1 Review, edge detectors.

questions.prompt: The highlighted lobe contains V1. Which comparison best captures the progression from early retinal processing to processing in V1?
choices: Retinal center-surround responses emphasize local light contrast; many V1 neurons are selective for oriented edges or bars.
Retinal ganglion cells primarily detect oriented bars; V1 neurons are the photoreceptors that first detect light.
Retinal and V1 responses encode the same feature in the same way; only their physical location changes.
Retinal ganglion cells already identify complete familiar objects; V1 primarily sends that identity back to the LGN.
questions.explanation: The review moves from center-surround ganglion-cell responses to orientation-selective V1 responses, illustrating changes in the visual information represented across stages.
choiceExplanations: This describes the review's progression from local contrast-sensitive retinal responses to edge and orientation selectivity in early visual cortex.
The course associates ganglion cells with center-surround responses and V1 with edge selectivity; photoreceptors are in the retina, not V1.
The review emphasizes changes in receptive-field organization and complexity across stages rather than identical processing in different places.
Ganglion-cell output is early visual information, not completed object recognition; the main pathway carries LGN output onward to V1.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 5: information detected across visual stages; Exam 1 Review, ganglion cells and V1.

questions.prompt: A display contains a red square and a green circle. What specifically is the binding problem for this display?
choices: How to detect that red and green are both present, without considering which shape has which color.
How separately represented colors and shapes are correctly assigned to the same objects.
How to locate the eyes relative to the stimulus so the image falls on the retina.
