How to choose a button after the correct colors and shapes have already been paired.
questions.explanation: Detecting red, green, square, and circle separately does not yet explain how red is assigned to the square and green to the circle as unified objects.
choiceExplanations: Feature detection alone leaves the problem unresolved: detecting both colors does not specify which color belongs to which shape.
The challenge is establishing which features belong together, so a red square and green circle are not confused with the opposite pairings.
Eye position affects visual input, but the binding problem specifically concerns relating the represented features into coherent objects.
Response selection can introduce its own demands, but it follows the correctly paired percept assumed here rather than explaining that pairing.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 5: the binding problem.

questions.prompt: To map the spatial extent of a hypothetical V1 neuron's receptive field, a researcher first finds a bar orientation that elicits a response. What should be varied next while gaze is held fixed?
choices: Only the bar's orientation at the same location, which maps all possible visual positions.
The observer's report of the object's name, while the stimulus never changes.
The bar's location across the visual field while its other relevant properties are kept comparable.
The time of day of recording, while neither the stimulus nor its position changes.
questions.explanation: A spatial receptive-field map requires sampling visual positions. Keeping a responsive feature and other conditions stable helps isolate location's effect on firing.
choiceExplanations: Varying orientation at one position estimates orientation tuning at that position; it does not identify the full spatial extent of responsiveness.
Naming reports do not replace the systematic variation of visual position needed to map the neuron's spatial receptive field.
This directly tests which locations influence the neuron while reducing confounds from changes in stimulus form or eye position.
Changing recording time does not systematically sample locations in the visual field and therefore does not provide the required spatial map.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 5: how researchers determine a receptive field.

questions.prompt: Consider an OFF-center/ON-surround ganglion cell in the simple center-surround model. Which equal-intensity light pattern should most strongly favor its response?
choices: A bright center surrounded by darkness.
The same steady light covering both center and surround uniformly.
A bright spot entirely outside the receptive field.
A dark center with illumination confined to the surrounding region.
questions.explanation: The OFF-center/ON-surround arrangement favors lower illumination in its center and greater illumination in its surround, the reverse of an ON-center/OFF-surround pattern.
choiceExplanations: A bright center with a dark surround favors the opposite center-surround arrangement and opposes the specified cell's preferred contrast.
Uniform light engages antagonistic center and surround influences, so it does not favor the response as strongly as the appropriate contrast pattern.
A spot outside the receptive field is not the effective stimulus for this neuron in the simplified receptive-field account.
This places darkness in the OFF-center and light in the ON-surround, combining the favorable influences in the simple model.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Exam 1 Review, center-surround ganglion cells and firing rates; Study Guide, Module 5.

questions.prompt: In a hypothetical case, a person can use a visible object's position to guide a reach but has unusual difficulty deciding whether it is a key or a comb. Which interpretation best uses the two-stream distinction?
choices: Ventral identity processing may be more disrupted than dorsal spatial/action processing in this task.
Dorsal processing must be more disrupted because the person cannot report the object's identity.
All visual input must be absent because recognition is difficult.
Both streams must be fully independent because their performance differs on these tasks.
questions.explanation: Relatively preserved visually guided action with impaired identity judgments fits a ventral-versus-dorsal distinction, without proving that the streams never interact.
choiceExplanations: The pattern contrasts impaired object identification with relatively preserved spatial guidance, matching the broad ventral and dorsal specializations.
Identity judgments are the broad ventral 'what' function, whereas the preserved spatially guided reach is associated with dorsal processing.
Using the object's visible position to guide the reach demonstrates some usable visual information, contradicting complete loss of input.
Different impairments support partial specialization, not absolute independence or the absence of connections between the streams.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 5: what and where pathways and evidence for their distinction.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical neuron later in the visual pathway responds to a complex pattern across a larger region of visual space than an earlier neuron. Which course principle best fits this observation?
choices: Later neurons must stop receiving any information that originated at the retina.
Receptive fields tend to become larger and selectivity can become more complex across successive stages.
Every later neuron must respond equally to all possible objects.
Larger receptive fields prove that only one neuron is needed for the entire visual experience.
questions.explanation: The review describes a progression from smaller fields and simple features toward larger fields and more complex patterns as information moves through the visual system.
choiceExplanations: Later stages transform and combine information derived from earlier processing; larger or more complex responses do not imply loss of all retinal influence.
This is the broad progression described in the review, without claiming that every neuron changes in exactly the same way.
Complex selectivity means different responses to different patterns, not necessarily equal responses to all objects.
One neuron's receptive field and selectivity do not establish that the entire scene is represented by a single cell.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Exam 1 Review, receptive fields across the visual system; Study Guide, Module 5.

questions.prompt: In a hypothetical recording, an ON-center/OFF-surround cell responds less to bright uniform illumination than to a dimmer spot confined to its center. Why is this compatible with the simple model?
choices: The cell's firing must be proportional only to the total light energy, so the observation cannot fit any center-surround account.
Surround illumination necessarily changes the cell into an OFF-center/ON-surround cell.
Uniform illumination activates opposing center and surround influences, so greater total light need not produce the greater response.
A dimmer spot produces larger individual action potentials, which is what response rate measures.
questions.explanation: Center-surround organization makes spatial contrast important. Antagonistic surround activity can reduce the response despite the greater total illumination of the whole field.
choiceExplanations: This ignores the antagonistic spatial arrangement; total photon count alone is not sufficient to predict the cell's response in this model.
Adding surround light changes the input pattern, not the neuron's fixed center-surround classification in the described experiment.
The center and surround contribute opposing effects, so the arrangement of illumination can matter more than its total amount.
Response rate counts spikes per time, not spike height; changing action-potential amplitude does not explain the specified firing-rate pattern.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Exam 1 Review, dot detectors and firing rates; Study Guide, Module 5: receptive fields.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical V1 neuron fires for a vertical bar on the left but not a horizontal bar on the right. Why do these two trials alone fail to establish that its receptive field excludes the right location?
choices: The response proves that orientation selectivity changes whenever the bar changes location.
The horizontal bar's failure is sufficient to exclude the right location regardless of other orientations.
The vertical bar's success is sufficient to establish responsiveness at every other location.
Both orientation and location changed; a poorly matched orientation could explain the weak right-side response.
questions.explanation: Spatial sensitivity and orientation tuning are confounded in this comparison. Testing a responsive orientation across positions would better isolate the receptive field's extent.
choiceExplanations: The trials do not compare multiple orientations within each location, so a location-dependent change in tuning has not been demonstrated.
The bar may be ineffective because of its orientation, so one such failure does not exclude responsiveness at that location to a better stimulus.
A response at one tested position cannot establish the spatial extent of the receptive field across untested positions.
Because two stimulus dimensions changed together, the result cannot uniquely attribute the response difference to spatial position.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 5: receptive-field mapping and tuning curves.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical experiment asks whether brief viewing impairs feature binding even when individual colors and shapes remain detectable. Which comparison most directly tests that claim?
choices: Use matched displays and exposure durations, comparing reports of which features were present with reports of which color belonged to which shape.
Compare color reports after a long exposure with shape reports after a short exposure, without asking about pairings.
Ask only whether any color was present, because successful color detection guarantees correct feature binding.
Compare naming a familiar object with detecting a bright light, then attribute every performance difference to binding.
questions.explanation: A binding-specific account needs to distinguish availability of the separate features from accuracy of their combinations. Matched input conditions help make that comparison interpretable.
choiceExplanations: This tests feature availability and correct assignment under comparable input conditions, allowing a selective pairing deficit to be identified.
Both feature type and exposure differ, and no pairing is tested; the comparison cannot specifically identify a problem in combining available features.
Detecting a color does not show that it was assigned to the correct shape, so this measure alone cannot test whether binding succeeded.
These tasks differ in many basic and higher-level demands; an uncontrolled difference would not isolate feature binding as its cause.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 105 Study Guide, Module 5: binding features into a coherent visual experience.

questions.prompt: Twelve identical dots are arranged with small gaps within each pair and large gaps between pairs. Which cue most directly makes the display look like six pairs?
choices: Proximity between neighboring dots.
Similarity between the colors of the dots.
Closure of incomplete contours.
Common movement of the dots.
questions.explanation: The informative difference is spacing: nearby elements group together by proximity. Because all dots look alike, similarity does not explain why these particular pairs form.
choiceExplanations: The smaller within-pair gaps provide the proximity cue that distinguishes each pair from its neighbors.
All twelve dots share their color, so color similarity cannot explain why only particular dots form pairs.
Closure concerns completing interrupted boundaries; this display supplies a spacing pattern, not incomplete outlines.
Common fate groups elements that move together, but no coordinated movement is described in this static display.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 6: Gestalt principles guiding form perception.

questions.prompt: In an evenly spaced grid, circles and triangles form alternating columns. The columns seem grouped by shape even though horizontal and vertical spacing are equal. Which principle best explains this?
choices: Proximity, because the vertical distances must be smaller.
Similarity, because elements within a column share a shape.
Common fate, because each column has a common destination.
Closure, because columns complete a missing boundary.
questions.explanation: Shape similarity can organize a display even when distance is matched. The grouping cue is shared appearance rather than spatial nearness or motion.
choiceExplanations: The question explicitly matches horizontal and vertical spacing, so smaller vertical gaps cannot explain the grouping.
Circles resemble other circles and triangles resemble other triangles, providing a similarity cue within each column.
Common fate refers to coordinated motion; merely belonging to a column does not supply a common-motion cue.
Closure involves completing incomplete shapes, whereas these columns are organized by the appearance of intact elements.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 6: Gestalt principles guiding form perception.

questions.prompt: Two smooth curved wires cross. A viewer tends to follow each wire smoothly through the crossing rather than perceive four segments that make abrupt turns. Which grouping principle is most relevant?
choices: Closure of a missing shape.
Similarity in surface brightness.
Good continuation of aligned contours.
Common fate of moving elements.
questions.explanation: Good continuation favors smoothly continuing contours. It helps determine which visible segments belong together when contours intersect or are interrupted.
choiceExplanations: No missing closed outline is required here; the decision concerns how visible contour segments continue through a crossing.
Brightness could sometimes aid grouping, but the described preference is specifically for smooth contour continuity.
Smoothly aligned segments are grouped as parts of the same contour rather than being joined into abrupt turns.
Common fate requires a shared motion pattern, which is absent from the description of the stationary wires.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 6: Gestalt principles guiding form perception.

questions.prompt: A logo consists of three separated line segments positioned like the sides of a triangle. Viewers perceive a complete triangular form despite gaps near its corners. This most directly illustrates:
choices: Motion parallax.
Binocular disparity.
Size constancy.
Closure.
questions.explanation: Closure organizes incomplete boundaries into a complete form. The example concerns grouping an interrupted contour, not estimating distance or preserving size across distances.
choiceExplanations: Motion parallax supplies depth information from relative image movement as an observer moves; no such movement occurs here.
Binocular disparity compares the two eyes' views, whereas the incomplete triangular form can be perceived with one eye.
Size constancy concerns stable perceived size despite retinal-size changes, not completing gaps in a contour.
The separated segments are organized into a complete bounded triangle, which is the relevant closure tendency.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 6: Gestalt principles guiding form perception.

questions.prompt: An ambiguous black-and-white image alternately appears to show a vase or two profiles. The contours stay fixed while which region seems to be the object changes. What is changing?
choices: Figure-ground assignment.
The distance between the two eyes.
The amount of observer motion.
The physical location of the contours.
questions.explanation: Figure-ground organization assigns regions and their borders to an object or its background. A stable image can support more than one such organization.
choiceExplanations: The viewer alternates which region owns the shared boundary and appears as the figure against a background.
The alternation does not require any change in eye separation; the ambiguity is in organizing the same image.
Observer movement is not described and is unnecessary for the competing figure-ground interpretations.
The question holds the contours fixed, so the change lies in perceptual organization rather than their physical positions.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 6: Gestalt form perception and figure-ground organization.

questions.prompt: With one eye closed, a passenger looks sideways from a slowly moving train. Nearby fence posts sweep across the view faster than distant hills. Which explanation best identifies the available depth information?
choices: Binocular disparity remains because the passenger knows where the closed eye is.
Motion parallax compares relative image changes during observer movement.
Linear perspective requires the fence posts to move faster than the hills.
Closure supplies depth by completing the gaps between the posts.
questions.explanation: Motion parallax is a monocular depth cue available across movement: nearer stationary objects generally change image position more rapidly than distant ones during observer translation.
choiceExplanations: Binocular disparity requires two simultaneous eye views; knowledge of the closed eye's position cannot replace its image.
The relative motion of nearby and distant scene elements during the train's movement supplies motion-parallax information.
Linear perspective uses projected convergence of lines, not the relative speed of image movement described here.
Closure concerns perceptual completion of boundaries and does not explain the distance-dependent motion pattern.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 6: monocular versus binocular depth cues.

questions.prompt: In a photograph of a tiled plaza, equally sized real tiles project as progressively smaller, denser patches toward the horizon. Which cue contributes to the impression of increasing distance?
choices: Common fate of the tiles.
Binocular disparity between the tiles.
Texture gradient across the surface.
Failure of figure-ground organization.
questions.explanation: A texture gradient uses systematic changes in projected texture size and density to signal surface depth. That pattern is available in a single photograph and to a single eye.
choiceExplanations: The tiles do not move together in the photograph, so common fate does not explain the static depth cue.
The relevant comparison is texture across one image, not differences between the two eyes' images of the scene.
Progressively smaller and denser projected texture elements provide information about a surface extending into depth.
The scene can be successfully organized into surfaces and objects; the depth impression does not require a segmentation failure.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 6: monocular depth cues.

questions.prompt: Identical dots are scattered randomly on a screen. Half begin drifting upward together and half drift downward together. Two groups become apparent although color and initial spacing do not distinguish them. What changed the grouping?
choices: A new similarity in dot shape.
A new difference in initial proximity.
Completion of a closed outer contour.
Shared motion within each set.
questions.explanation: Common fate groups elements with coordinated motion. It can reveal groups that static appearance and initial spatial arrangement do not distinguish.
choiceExplanations: All dots retain the same appearance; a change in dot shape cannot explain the newly apparent motion groups.
The question holds the initial spacing uninformative, so proximity is not the newly introduced organizing cue.
The moving dots need not form a closed outline; their shared direction of movement is sufficient for this grouping tendency.
Dots moving in the same direction group by common fate, separating the upward-moving and downward-moving sets.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 6: Gestalt principles, including common fate.

questions.prompt: A round plate viewed at an angle projects an ellipse onto the retina, yet the observer describes the plate itself as circular. Which statement correctly separates input from perception?
choices: The retinal projection is elliptical while perceived object shape remains approximately circular.
Shape constancy changes the retinal projection back into a circle.
The observer must be using only binocular information to perceive the plate as circular.
Perceiving a circle proves that the plate's retinal image cannot affect recognition.
questions.explanation: Shape constancy concerns an object's perceived shape across viewpoint-dependent image changes. It does not require the retinal projection itself to stay constant.
choiceExplanations: The observer can interpret an elliptical projection as the image of a tilted circular object, illustrating shape constancy.
Perceptual interpretation does not physically undo the projection produced by the plate's orientation relative to the eye.
Shape constancy can use monocular context and shape information; it is not restricted to binocular cues.
The image remains evidence for orientation and shape; constancy is an interpretation of that evidence rather than its absence.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 6: perceptual constancy.

questions.prompt: A participant views an ordinary flat photograph through a small opening with one eye. One depicted chair partly hides another, and the participant reports that the hiding chair is nearer. What can this result establish?
choices: Occlusion can specify which chair is nearer only if both eyes are open.
A monocular occlusion cue can support relative depth even without stereo images of the depicted scene.
Because the photograph is flat, familiarity with chairs must be the sole source of the depth impression.
The occlusion relation supplies the chairs' exact viewing distances as well as their near-far order.
questions.explanation: Interposition supplies ordinal depth information: the occluding object is usually interpreted as nearer. A depth impression does not establish binocular input, physical depth in the photograph, or exact metric distance.
choiceExplanations: Occlusion is visible in a single eye's image; interpreting its relative depth information does not require comparing two eyes.
The depicted overlap provides a nearer-versus-farther relation even though no stereo pair of the chairs is presented.
Flat images still contain pictorial depth information such as overlap; familiarity is not the only available information here.
Occlusion supplies relative ordering, but by itself it does not specify how many meters separate the observer and chairs.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 6: monocular depth cues and interpretation of visual input.

questions.prompt: Two disks subtend the same visual angle. Reliable scene cues make disk A appear farther away than disk B. Under size-distance scaling, which perceived-size prediction follows?
choices: A should appear smaller because the farther disk's equal retinal extent is interpreted as a smaller object.
They should appear equal because equal retinal extents outweigh any difference in inferred distance.
A should appear larger because the same retinal extent at greater inferred distance implies a larger object.
Their perceived distances should become equal because equal visual angles imply equal viewing distances.
questions.explanation: Perceived size depends on both image size and interpreted distance. Holding visual angle constant, an object interpreted as farther away can be perceived as physically larger.
choiceExplanations: This confuses the retinal shrinkage of a fixed object moving away with the present case, which holds retinal extent constant.
Perceptual constancy demonstrates that perceived object size is not determined by retinal extent alone; distance information matters.
A larger physical object is needed to occupy the same visual angle at a greater distance, motivating the predicted larger appearance.
Equal visual angles can arise from different combinations of size and distance, so they do not force equal inferred distances.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 6: perceptual size constancy and depth information.

questions.prompt: The same blurry object is initially identified differently when shown in a kitchen scene versus a workshop scene. When its diagnostic edges become sharp, observers correctly identify it in both scenes. What joint account best explains both stages?
choices: Context determines perception entirely, so sharpening the edges should have no effect.
The final agreement shows that context had no effect on the earlier ambiguous image.
Bottom-up processing means context can influence responses only after perception is finished.
Top-down context biases ambiguous evidence, while stronger bottom-up evidence can overcome that bias.
questions.explanation: Top-down and bottom-up influences interact. Context is useful when sensory evidence is ambiguous, but improved diagnostic input can constrain or reverse an initially plausible interpretation.
choiceExplanations: An entirely context-determined account cannot explain why improved edge evidence makes the interpretations converge across scenes.
Later agreement does not erase the earlier contextual difference; the two stages show that the balance of evidence can change.
Bottom-up processing names the sensory contribution, not a rule forbidding context from influencing perceptual interpretation.
This account explains both the initial scene-dependent guesses and the correction when diagnostic sensory features become clear.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 6: bottom-up versus top-down processing.

questions.prompt: In a feature-net model, what does it mean for a detector to have a lower recognition threshold?
choices: Less activation is required before that detector signals recognition.
The stimulus must contain fewer physical features than every competing stimulus.
The detector can no longer receive bottom-up evidence.
Its recognition decision is guaranteed to be correct.
questions.explanation: A threshold is an activation criterion. A lower threshold allows recognition with weaker additional evidence, which can improve detection but also permit errors when the candidate is wrong.
choiceExplanations: The detector reaches its decision criterion with less activation; the change concerns processing rather than the physical stimulus.
Threshold and feature count are different quantities; lowering a criterion does not remove features from the displayed object.
A detector can still receive sensory evidence after its threshold changes, and that evidence can still constrain recognition.
An easier-to-reach threshold can favor a wrong candidate under ambiguity, so lower threshold does not guarantee accuracy.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 7: feature nets, ambiguity, errors, and priming.

questions.prompt: Which comparison best captures how Recognition by Components extends the idea of combining simpler visual features?
choices: RBC replaces all shape information with familiar object names.
RBC emphasizes three-dimensional components and their arrangement, rather than only a list of simple image features.
RBC requires a complete new representation for every pixel change.
RBC assumes each object consists of one indivisible feature.
questions.explanation: Both approaches build recognition from simpler constituents. RBC specifically emphasizes reusable volumetric components, or geons, and the structural relations among them.
choiceExplanations: RBC is a structural shape account; naming an object does not replace the need to represent its components and relations.
Geons provide volumetric building blocks, and their spatial relations specify how those parts form a particular object.
RBC seeks some robustness across changing images through stable structure, rather than storing every exact pixel arrangement.
The account explicitly decomposes objects into components, so treating every object as indivisible reverses its proposal.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 7: RBC and its relationship to feature nets.

questions.prompt: Two unfamiliar constructions contain the same cylinder and rectangular block, but the cylinder rests on top of the block in one and attaches to its side in the other. What must an RBC representation retain to distinguish them?
choices: Only the number of components.
Only the components' average brightness.
The spatial relation between the components.
Only whether the image has been seen before.
questions.explanation: A list of parts is insufficient when objects share components. RBC includes relations among the parts, allowing different arrangements of the same components to represent different objects.
choiceExplanations: Both constructions contain two components, so their component counts cannot distinguish the top-versus-side arrangements.
Brightness is not the specified difference, and it does not encode where the cylinder is attached relative to the block.
The on-top-of versus attached-to-the-side relation distinguishes the constructions despite their shared component inventory.
Familiarity alone does not specify structural identity; both can be unfamiliar yet visibly different in component arrangement.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 7: Recognition by Components and structural relations.

questions.prompt: Which representation most directly supports a viewpoint-dependent account of object recognition?
choices: A representation containing only an object's usual spoken name.
A representation that discards all information about learned appearances.
A structural description assumed to work identically from every possible view.
Representations of learned appearances that match some viewing angles better than others.
questions.explanation: Viewpoint-dependent recognition is sensitive to the relation between the current image and learned views. Recognition can therefore become less efficient as the appearance departs from those views.
choiceExplanations: A spoken name alone does not specify the visual appearance differences that make some viewing angles easier to recognize.
Discarding learned appearance information would remove the basis for the trained-view advantage described by this account.
Identical performance at every angle is not the defining prediction of a viewpoint-dependent account.
Stored or learned appearances can fit familiar angles better, creating costs for images farther from the learned views.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 7: viewpoint-dependent recognition.

questions.prompt: A feature net mistakenly identifies a noisy unfamiliar symbol as a familiar symbol. Keeping the model's thresholds fixed, which change most directly supplies evidence that could correct the error?
choices: Reveal a diagnostic feature that favors the unfamiliar symbol over the familiar candidate.
Increase prior activation of the familiar candidate while leaving the image unchanged.
Remove the few visible features that distinguish the symbols.
Treat whichever candidate is familiar as correct regardless of sensory evidence.
questions.explanation: More diagnostic bottom-up evidence can shift competition toward the correct candidate. Priming can help recognition, but familiarity should not be treated as a substitute for matching the actual stimulus.
choiceExplanations: A distinguishing feature adds evidence for the correct candidate and against the mistaken familiar interpretation.
Further activating the already favored wrong candidate would strengthen the bias rather than supply corrective evidence.
Removing discriminating features makes the input more ambiguous and generally leaves less evidence to correct the mistake.
Familiarity is a processing bias, not a definition of truth; this rule would preserve the error when the unfamiliar symbol is present.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 7: feature-net ambiguity and recognition errors.

questions.prompt: A person recognizes a colleague immediately by voice and accurately names ordinary objects, but repeatedly fails to identify the colleague from their face. Which interpretation best fits this selective pattern?
choices: The colleague's identity has been lost from every form of recognition.
Face-based identity recognition may be disproportionately impaired despite preserved recognition through other cues.
All visual shape processing must be absent because faces are visual objects.
Preserved voice recognition rules out any difficulty recognizing faces.
questions.explanation: The pattern is consistent with a selective face-recognition impairment, as in prosopagnosia. Preserved recognition by voice argues against loss of all knowledge of the person; a vignette alone is not a clinical diagnosis.
choiceExplanations: Successful recognition by voice shows that at least one route to the colleague's identity remains available.
The contrast specifically implicates using facial appearance for identity, while other recognition abilities remain relatively spared.
Naming ordinary objects provides evidence for preserved visual recognition, so the deficit cannot simply be all visual shape processing.
Face and voice recognition need not fail together; recognizing someone through sound can coexist with impaired face identification.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 7: special properties of face recognition.

questions.prompt: Two face images contain exactly the same eyes, nose, and mouth, but the distances between those parts differ. Observers readily distinguish the faces. Which information must contribute beyond the mere presence of the parts?
choices: Only the total number of facial features.
Only the average brightness of the image.
The configuration or spacing of facial features.
Only whether the image is labeled as a face.
questions.explanation: Configural processing uses relationships among facial parts. Identical parts can produce a different perceived face when their arrangement changes.
choiceExplanations: The images have the same feature inventory and count, so counting eyes, noses, and mouths cannot distinguish them.
The diagnostic manipulation is part spacing; average brightness need not change when the parts are rearranged.
Relative spacing distinguishes the images even though each individual part is unchanged, demonstrating configural information.
Both stimuli are faces, so a shared category label does not explain how observers tell these two particular images apart.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 7: face recognition and configural processing.

questions.prompt: Two masks hide equal amounts of an object's image. Mask A preserves the contours and junctions needed to identify its volumetric components; mask B hides that diagnostic structure. What does RBC predict, other things being equal?
choices: Equal performance because only the percentage of visible pixels matters.
Better performance with B because component information is irrelevant to RBC.
Failure with both because RBC requires a completely unobscured image.
Better recognition with A because recoverable components and relations matter more than visible area alone.
questions.explanation: A component account depends on diagnostic structural information. Equal visible area need not mean equal recognition if one mask preserves the evidence needed to recover the parts and their arrangement.
choiceExplanations: Equal visible area does not guarantee equal diagnostic information; RBC weights recoverable structure rather than pixel count alone.
Components are central to RBC, so hiding the information needed to recover them should not improve recognition for that reason.
RBC can support recognition from incomplete input when enough diagnostic components and relations remain recoverable.
Mask A preserves the structural cues on which RBC relies, making better recognition plausible despite equal amounts of occlusion.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 7: RBC, component recovery, and recognition across changed views.

questions.prompt: Group A learns an unfamiliar object at 0 degrees and group B learns it at 60 degrees. Diagnostic components are visible at both test views. Each group recognizes its own trained view faster. Which feature of the result most directly supports viewpoint dependence?
choices: The easiest view changes with training history even though diagnostic components remain visible.
The result is explained by one intrinsically easier viewing angle, independently of what each group learned.
Preserving components is sufficient to explain why each group favors its own trained angle.
The trained-view advantage identifies deliberate mental rotation as the mechanism rather than learned-view matching.
questions.explanation: Reversing which view is favored through training ties performance to learned appearance rather than an intrinsically superior view. It supports viewpoint dependence without proving that structural information never contributes.
choiceExplanations: The preferred view follows experience rather than a fixed angle, and preserved components reduce a simple hidden-parts explanation.
The preferred angle reverses between groups, so one intrinsically easier angle independent of experience cannot explain both results.
Both views preserve components, so visibility alone does not explain why the faster view changes with training history.
A familiarity-related advantage does not uniquely identify deliberate mental rotation; multiple view-dependent processes could produce it.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 7: contrast viewpoint-dependent recognition with RBC.

questions.prompt: In a simplified feature net, each detector reports recognition at activation 10. A noisy square supplies 9 units to the square detector and 5 to the circle detector. An earlier prime leaves 6 residual units only in the circle detector. If activation adds without decay, what response is predicted immediately after the target?
choices: Square, because its current sensory evidence of 9 is stronger than the circle detector's current evidence of 5.
Circle, because residual activation raises it to 11 despite the stronger current evidence favoring square.
Neither shape, because neither receives 10 activation units from the current target alone.
Both shapes, because their combined activation of 20 equals the sum of their two thresholds.
questions.explanation: The circle detector reaches 6 + 5 = 11 and crosses its threshold, while the square detector reaches only 9. The model therefore makes a priming-related error: the actual square gives more current evidence to square, but residual activation favors the wrong candidate.
choiceExplanations: This compares current evidence alone and ignores the six residual units; square remains below its own threshold of ten.
Circle's residual six plus current five yields eleven, so it crosses threshold and produces an incorrect circle report.
The stated model adds residual activation to current evidence; a detector need not receive all ten units from the target alone.
Each detector must reach its own threshold; pooling activation across different candidates cannot make the square detector reach ten.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 7: feature nets and priming. Activation values are illustrative.

questions.prompt: In a dichotic-listening study, a participant is asked to shadow the message presented to the left ear. What task are they being asked to perform?
choices: Alternate freely between both messages and summarize their combined meaning.
Watch for changes in the position of a visual target.
Repeat the selected left-ear message aloud as it is heard.
Report only the loudness of the unattended right-ear message.
questions.explanation: Shadowing is continuous repetition of a selected spoken message. It provides an ongoing task that directs attention toward one channel while investigators examine processing of another.
choiceExplanations: Freely switching or combining both streams would not maintain the prescribed selection of the left-ear message.
This describes a visual monitoring task rather than repetition of an auditory message in dichotic listening.
Repeating the designated message as it arrives is shadowing and helps sustain attention to the selected channel.
The unattended channel may be probed experimentally, but loudness reporting is not the requested shadowing task.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 8: evidence concerning selective attention and selection models.

questions.prompt: Which claim distinguishes late selection from a strict early filter?
choices: Input is selected exclusively by physical channel before meaning can be analyzed.
An unattended message is physically removed before reaching the ear.
Every processed word must be consciously reported immediately.
Meaning can be analyzed before selection determines what guides a report or response.
questions.explanation: Late selection places the major selection boundary after more semantic processing. Processing meaning and selecting an item for conscious report are not the same event.
choiceExplanations: Selecting physical channels before full meaning analysis describes the strict early-filter alternative, not late selection.
These theories concern internal processing limits; they do not require the unattended sound to be physically removed from the ear.
Late selection separates semantic processing from report, so it does not imply immediate conscious reporting of all processed words.
Allowing semantic analysis before selection for a response or awareness is the defining late-selection contrast.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 8: early versus late selection.

questions.prompt: In an attenuation model, which combination makes an unattended item most likely to reach recognition?
choices: Some weakened input survives, and that item's recognition threshold is low enough for the surviving activation.
No activation survives, and every item has the same positive threshold.
Input is weakened, and recognition thresholds become infinitely high.
Every unattended item is strengthened until it receives full conscious attention.
questions.explanation: Attenuation reduces signal strength without requiring complete elimination. Threshold differences explain why selected items can break through a weakened channel more readily than others.
choiceExplanations: Surviving weak activation can still exceed a sufficiently low threshold, allowing selective unattended-item recognition.
With no surviving activation and a positive threshold, there is no signal available to reach recognition in this account.
An infinitely high threshold prevents recognition regardless of the weakened input, contrary to the requested breakthrough.
Attenuation does not require boosting all unattended material to full awareness; that would remove its selective-weakening mechanism.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 8: attenuation compared with early and late selection.

questions.prompt: In the course's two-priming account, which effect can occur even when a cue is too unreliable to justify deliberately preparing for its predicted target?
choices: Strategic preparation must consume resources on every trial regardless of cue reliability.
Features activated by the cue can facilitate a related target without an added cost to unrelated targets.
Unrelated targets must always be slower than a neutral baseline.
A related target can be facilitated only if the participant consciously expects it.
questions.explanation: Stimulus-driven priming follows activation from the input and is described as cost-free in this course model. It need not depend on useful predictive expectations.
choiceExplanations: Expectation-based preparation depends on strategic use of predictions; an unreliable cue need not prompt the same allocation.
Bottom-up activation can facilitate related detectors despite poor predictiveness, without the invalid-trial cost of strategic allocation.
The course distinguishes stimulus-driven facilitation from expectation costs; unrelated targets need not be impaired in this case.
Stimulus-driven priming does not require conscious target expectation, which is the key contrast with deliberate preparation.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 8; 105 Exam 1 Review, slides 17–20: stimulus-driven and expectation-based priming.

questions.prompt: While a participant shadows one message, an unattended word changes how they interpret an ambiguous word in the attended message. Suppose physical differences and brief attention shifts have been carefully controlled. Which claim is most directly challenged?
choices: Attended words can receive semantic processing.
Meaning can influence interpretation of another word.
Unattended input is completely excluded before any meaning analysis.
A response can depend on more than one source of evidence.
questions.explanation: A controlled meaning-dependent effect from unattended material conflicts with complete presemantic exclusion. It does not, by itself, determine that every unattended word is fully analyzed or consciously experienced.
choiceExplanations: The attended word's interpretation is being measured, so the result does not challenge its access to semantic processing.
The unattended word's meaning-dependent influence supports, rather than challenges, an effect of meaning on interpretation.
If meaning from the unattended stream affects interpretation, that stream cannot have been entirely blocked before meaning analysis.
The response's sensitivity to both streams is evidence for combined influences, not evidence that only one source can matter.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 8: evidence distinguishing selection models.

questions.prompt: During shadowing, a participant notices that the unattended voice changes pitch but cannot report the words it spoke. What distinction does this observation most directly demonstrate?
choices: Every unnoticed word must have been consciously understood.
Detecting pitch requires understanding the message's semantic content.
The unattended sound never entered the auditory system.
Sensitivity to physical properties can coexist with poor report of message content.
questions.explanation: Physical-change detection and content report are different measures. The pattern is consistent with early physical selection, but poor word report alone does not prove that absolutely no semantic processing occurred.
choiceExplanations: The result establishes no conscious understanding of every word; it reports pitch detection and limited word report only.
Pitch is a physical property of the sound, and detecting a pitch change does not require identifying the words' meanings.
Noticing the pitch change demonstrates that some information from the unattended sound was registered.
The participant detects an acoustic change while reporting little content, separating physical sensitivity from explicit word report.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 8: early-selection evidence from unattended-channel processing.

questions.prompt: A cue initially predicts the target accurately on 80% of trials, then becomes accurate on only 20%. After participants learn the new reliability, what change does the course's strategic-priming account predict, with sensory cue features held fixed?
choices: Less preparation for the cued target and a smaller expectation-related penalty when a different target appears.
Stronger preparation for the cued target because unreliable information is more useful.
Loss of every stimulus-driven effect because physical cue features no longer exist.
The same strategic allocation is required because expectations cannot change with experience.
questions.explanation: Useful predictive cues encourage expectation-based preparation. Once the cue becomes unreliable, preparing specifically for its indicated target is less useful, so its expectation-related invalid cost should diminish; stimulus-driven activation may remain.
choiceExplanations: Reduced trust in the indicated target should reduce resource allocation toward it and the cost of being misled by that indication.
The cued target is now rarely correct; this does not justify stronger preparation for that same indicated target.
Cue features are explicitly unchanged, so their bottom-up activation can remain even when strategic expectations change.
Expectation-based priming is sensitive to predictive usefulness; treating allocation as fixed ignores the reliability manipulation.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 8; 105 Exam 1 Review, slides 18–20: low- and high-validity cue effects.

questions.prompt: Two identical weak targets are presented in otherwise matched trials. The observer expects one target category and recognizes it more often. In the course's detector account, what can explain the improvement without changing the physical target?
choices: Expectation must increase the target's actual luminance.
Top-down preparation can make the expected detector easier to bring to recognition threshold.
An expected target no longer needs any information from the eyes.
Higher recognition proves that unexpected categories receive exactly the same preparation.
questions.explanation: Expectation-based priming prepares detectors for likely input. The same sensory evidence can therefore reach recognition more readily without a physical change in the stimulus.
choiceExplanations: The physical targets are held identical; an internal expectation need not change the light emitted by the display.
Preparing the relevant detector changes its readiness, allowing the same weak input to support recognition more readily.
Preparation combines with incoming evidence; it does not establish that seeing the presented target no longer requires visual input.
Selective preparation can favor the expected category, and the benefit does not establish equal preparation of alternatives.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 8; 105 Exam 1 Review, slide 17: thresholds and expectation-based priming.

questions.prompt: A priming graph uses the review slide's convention: plotted value = neutral RT minus condition RT. An invalid-cue bar is −45 ms. Assuming comparable accuracy, what does that bar mean?
choices: Invalid responses were 45 ms faster than neutral, a benefit.
The participant responded 45 ms before the stimulus appeared.
Invalid responses were 45 ms slower than neutral, an invalid-cue cost.
Valid responses were 45 ms faster than invalid responses.
questions.explanation: If neutral minus invalid equals −45, invalid equals neutral plus 45. The negative plotted value therefore denotes slower responses to invalid targets, not negative raw reaction times.
choiceExplanations: A faster invalid response would make neutral minus invalid positive; the negative sign here indicates the opposite relationship.
The plotted number is a difference between mean reaction times, not a raw response time measured before stimulus onset.
Rearranging neutral − invalid = −45 gives invalid = neutral + 45, so the invalid condition carries a 45 ms cost.
The bar compares invalid with neutral only; the valid condition's response time is not supplied by this number.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Exam 1 Review, slide 20: neutral-minus-condition plotting convention. Values are hypothetical.

questions.prompt: A researcher claims that hearing one's name in a nominally unattended message proves that all unattended words receive full semantic processing. Which additional observation most directly raises an alternative explanation involving attention shifts?
choices: The name and other words are presented at equal loudness.
The listener can identify words in the message they are supposed to shadow.
The name has the same number of syllables as a comparison word.
Name reports occur mainly on trials when shadowing of the designated channel briefly breaks down.
questions.explanation: A lapse in shadowing around the reported name is consistent with temporary reallocation of attention. Name detection is therefore not sufficient to infer full processing of every genuinely unattended word.
choiceExplanations: Matching loudness reduces a physical-salience confound, but it does not directly show whether attention left the designated stream.
Good report of attended words confirms processing of the selected channel, not an attention shift toward the unattended one.
Matching syllable count controls one stimulus property without directly measuring whether the listener changed attentional focus.
The coupling between shadowing lapses and name reports suggests that the supposedly unattended stream sometimes became attended.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 8: evaluating evidence for early, late, and attenuated selection.

questions.prompt: Two cue conditions both produce a 30 ms valid-target benefit relative to neutral. Condition A has no invalid-target cost; condition B has a 40 ms invalid-target cost. Accuracy is matched. Which interpretation fits the course's priming distinction best?
choices: The equal benefits conceal a difference: B provides evidence for costly expectation-based allocation that A's benefit alone does not establish.
Equal valid benefits prove that the same amount and type of attention were used.
Condition A must involve more strategic allocation because its invalid targets are not slowed.
The invalid costs can be ignored because only valid trials distinguish the two priming types.
questions.explanation: A benefit alone does not identify its mechanism. In this course model, impairment of unexpected targets relative to neutral is informative evidence for resource allocation, even when valid benefits are equal.
choiceExplanations: B's extra impairment of unexpected targets is evidence for costly preparation; A remains compatible with cost-free stimulus-driven facilitation.
The invalid conditions differ substantially, so equal valid benefits cannot establish identical processing mechanisms.
Absence of an invalid cost does not establish greater strategic allocation; such costs are a key sign of misallocated expectation.
The course explicitly uses benefits and costs together to distinguish priming accounts, making the invalid trials informative.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 8; 105 Exam 1 Review, slides 17–20: priming benefits and costs. Values are hypothetical.

questions.prompt: A person keeps their eyes on a central fixation mark while mentally prioritizing a location to the right. Which description correctly names this change?
choices: An eye movement to the right-hand location.
A covert shift of spatial attention without changing gaze.
A loss of visual input from the left half of the retina.
A requirement that every right-hand object be consciously identified.
questions.explanation: Attention and eye position can be separated. Covert attention prioritizes a location while gaze remains fixed, which is why fixation-controlled cueing studies can test attention beyond eye movements.
choiceExplanations: The eyes remain at fixation by definition, so the spatial priority change is not itself an overt eye movement.
The observer changes which location receives processing priority without moving their eyes, the definition of covert orienting.
Shifting attentional priority does not require eliminating retinal input from the opposite side of the visual field.
Prioritizing a region can improve processing without guaranteeing complete conscious identification of every object there.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 9; 105 Exam 1 Review, slide 22: spatial attention and Posner cueing.

questions.prompt: The exam review describes neglect as reduced responding to contralesional space and excessive orientation toward ipsilesional space. In a case with a right-hemisphere lesion, which side pairing matches that description?
choices: Reduced responding on the right; excessive orientation left.
Reduced responding above fixation; excessive orientation below.
Reduced responding on the left; excessive orientation right.
Equal neglect of both sides because the lesion is unilateral.
questions.explanation: Contralesional means opposite the lesion and ipsilesional means on its side. Thus the described right-lesion pattern concerns reduced attention to left space and increased orientation to right space.
choiceExplanations: This reverses the side terms: for a right-sided lesion, left space is contralesional and right space is ipsilesional.
Above and below describe a different spatial axis; they do not implement the lesion-side comparison in this example.
Left is opposite the right-sided lesion, while right is on the lesion's side, matching the stated neglect pattern.
The review's description is spatially biased rather than an assertion that every unilateral lesion produces equal bilateral neglect.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Exam 1 Review, slide 23: hemispatial neglect as evidence for spatial attention.

questions.prompt: In Feature Integration Theory, what additional information is needed to conclude that a particular item is both green and triangular?
choices: Only evidence that green occurs somewhere in the display.
Only evidence that a triangle occurs somewhere in the display.
The average brightness across the entire display.
Evidence that the color and shape belong to the same object or location.
questions.explanation: Detecting individual features does not specify their ownership. Binding assigns the color and shape to a common item, rather than combining features that occur on separate objects.
choiceExplanations: Green could belong to a different item; detecting a color somewhere does not establish the target's color-shape conjunction.
A triangle could have another color, so its presence alone cannot establish that a green triangle is present.
Average brightness does not tell which object owns the detected color or shape and cannot resolve the conjunction.
Assigning both features to the same item supplies the binding information needed to identify a green triangle.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 9: Feature Integration Theory and attention's role in binding.

questions.prompt: In the classic FIT account, which operation is most closely associated with the initial parallel feature-processing stage?
choices: Registering basic properties such as color or orientation across the display before full object-level binding.
Guaranteeing conscious identification of every object in the display.
Selecting a different spoken response for every displayed item simultaneously.
Assigning every detected feature to the correct object without any role for attention.
questions.explanation: Classic FIT distinguishes early feature registration from attention-dependent binding. Parallel feature detection does not imply unlimited conscious identification or error-free feature ownership.
choiceExplanations: The initial stage registers separable basic features, while additional binding is needed to specify which features belong together.
Registering basic features is not the same as consciously identifying every complete object in the scene.
Spoken response selection is a later task demand, not the feature-registration operation proposed by classic FIT.
The theory gives attention a role in correct feature binding, so error-free ownership without attention contradicts that distinction.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 9: Feature Integration Theory.

questions.prompt: A cue and a target stay at exactly the same screen locations. The target is faster to detect when contours connect it to the cued object than when those contours make it part of a different object. What does the contour manipulation add to a purely spatial account?
choices: It shows that cue-target distance became shorter despite unchanged locations.
It shows that object organization can influence priority even when the relevant spatial coordinates are fixed.
It establishes that spatial attention never occurs.
It proves that every feature of the cued object is fully processed.
questions.explanation: Changing object membership while holding locations fixed tests whether object structure contributes beyond coordinates alone. A benefit tied to grouping supports an object-based contribution without excluding spatial selection.
choiceExplanations: The locations are held fixed, so a shorter cue-target distance is not available to explain the performance difference.
The changed contours alter which object contains the target, demonstrating an influence of grouping beyond the fixed coordinates.
An object-based contribution can coexist with spatial prioritization; this result does not eliminate spatial attention.
Faster target detection measures a priority benefit, not complete processing of every possible feature of the object.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 9: evidence for object-based attention.

questions.prompt: In a fixation-controlled cueing task, the identical left-side target is detected faster after a left cue than after a right cue. Accuracy is comparable and eye tracking confirms no gaze shift. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: The left cue physically moves the target toward the fovea.
The target must be brighter after the left cue.
Spatial preparation can improve processing at the target location independently of an eye movement.
A right cue permanently blocks all sensory input from the left.
questions.explanation: The sensory target and eye position are controlled, so the cue-dependent response difference supports covert spatial prioritization. It does not require a change in brightness or complete loss of uncued input.
choiceExplanations: Neither target position nor gaze changes, so retinal repositioning toward the fovea cannot explain the cue effect.
The target is physically identical across conditions; the manipulation concerns preparation rather than luminance.
A performance benefit with fixed target and gaze positions supports an attentional change in priority at that location.
Slower detection of an uncued target does not establish permanent sensory blockage; the participant still detects it.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 9; 105 Exam 1 Review, slide 22: Posner spatial cueing.

questions.prompt: After a brief display, viewers accurately report which colors and shapes occurred, but an added attention task increases mistakes about which color belonged to which shape. What is the most specific deficit suggested by this pattern?
choices: Complete loss of color detection.
Complete loss of shape detection.
Failure to detect that any visual stimulus appeared.
Impaired assignment of detected features to the same objects.
questions.explanation: Preserved feature inventories with incorrect pairings isolate a binding problem more specifically than a failure to register the features. Classic FIT predicts that reduced attention can increase such conjunction errors.
choiceExplanations: The viewers accurately report which colors were present, so a complete failure of color detection does not fit the evidence.
The shapes are also reported correctly as an inventory, arguing against complete loss of shape detection.
Accurate reports of the displayed features demonstrate that the display was detected and processed to some extent.
The errors concern ownership of already detected features, precisely the binding operation emphasized by Feature Integration Theory.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 9: Feature Integration Theory and illusory conjunctions.

questions.prompt: With accuracy held steady, increasing a display from 6 to 18 items adds 24 ms to a unique-feature search but 240 ms to a conjunction search. Which interpretation is appropriately limited?
choices: The 2 versus 20 ms-per-item slopes fit greater attentional demands in conjunction search, without proving one rigid search mechanism for every display.
The slopes are 24 and 240 ms per item because those are the total increases.
The smaller feature slope proves that every distractor was consciously recognized at the same time.
The larger conjunction slope proves that the eyes moved to every item.
questions.explanation: The set-size change is 12 items, so the slopes are 24/12 = 2 and 240/12 = 20 ms per item. The contrast fits classic FIT but does not by itself establish conscious processing or a particular eye-movement sequence.
choiceExplanations: The computed slopes show a larger set-size cost for conjunction search, which supports the classic distinction without overclaiming its mechanism.
A slope divides the change in response time by the change in item count; using total time increases omits the twelve-item denominator.
A shallow response-time slope does not measure conscious recognition of every distractor and cannot establish that stronger claim.
Response-time slopes do not directly measure gaze, so no specific sequence of eye movements follows from these data alone.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 9: feature versus conjunction search. Numerical data are hypothetical.

questions.prompt: A study reports faster responses to targets on the cued object than on another object. However, same-object targets are always closer to the cue. Which change is most important before interpreting the advantage as object-based attention?
choices: Recruit more participants using the same unmatched layout so the same-object advantage is estimated more precisely.
Compare same-object and different-object targets at matched cue-target distances while controlling other display differences.
Replace response time with accuracy while retaining the same distance difference between the two conditions.
Compare same-object trials with no-cue trials, without adding an equally distant different-object comparison.
questions.explanation: Object membership is confounded with spatial distance. Matching distance allows the comparison to test whether membership contributes beyond a straightforward spatial advantage.
choiceExplanations: A larger sample can estimate the confounded effect more precisely, but it cannot separate object membership from distance.
Equal-distance comparisons remove the obvious spatial explanation and make an object-membership effect more informative.
Spatial distance can influence accuracy as well as response time, so changing the outcome measure does not remove the confound.
A no-cue comparison can measure cueing benefit, but without the matched different-object condition it cannot isolate object membership.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 9: evidence for spatial versus object-based attention.

questions.prompt: Display A contains a red circle and a blue square; display B contains a blue circle and a red square. Both contain exactly one of each color and shape. Why is knowing the feature totals insufficient to decide which display contains a red square?
choices: The two displays differ only in the number of colors.
Neither display contains enough visual information to answer the question.
The decision requires the pairing of color and shape within objects, not just the presence of those features somewhere.
Counting features automatically identifies their object membership without attention.
questions.explanation: The feature inventories are identical, but their pairings differ. Identifying the red square requires binding red and square to the same item, which occurs in display B.
choiceExplanations: Both displays contain the same two colors in the same counts, so color number does not distinguish the target's presence.
The displays do contain the relevant pairings; the limitation concerns feature totals, not absence of visual evidence.
Only the relation between features identifies whether red and square belong together, making binding necessary for this judgment.
A count loses ownership information: one red and one square do not tell whether they occur on the same object.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 9: Feature Integration Theory and the binding problem.

questions.prompt: The exam review identifies a response selector as a task-general resource. Which operation best matches its stated role?
choices: Encoding only the pitch of an auditory stimulus.
Detecting only the orientation of a visual edge.
Maintaining the optical focus of the lens.
Choosing and initiating the appropriate response to a task event.
questions.explanation: Response selection concerns deciding and initiating what to do. Different sensory tasks can both need this shared stage even when their modality-specific perceptual demands differ.
choiceExplanations: Pitch encoding is auditory processing, whereas the response selector concerns choosing and initiating actions across tasks.
Visual-edge detection is a sensory operation and does not by itself specify which task response should be made.
Optical focusing changes the eye's image formation and is not the task-general response-selection function in the review.
Selecting and initiating the required response is the review's stated function of this shared processing resource.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Exam 1 Review, slide 26: task-general response selection and executive control.

questions.prompt: Which demand most directly calls on executive control as described in the divided-attention review?
choices: Replacing an old task rule with a new priority while suppressing the habitual response.
Representing the wavelength of incoming light before any task goal is considered.
Determining whether two retinal images contain binocular disparity.
Grouping nearby dots solely from their spatial arrangement.
questions.explanation: Executive control helps set goals and priorities and overcome habits. Rule changes especially expose the need to coordinate behavior with current goals rather than continue a previously useful response.
choiceExplanations: Changing the governing rule and resisting the old habit directly require the goal-setting and control functions emphasized in the review.
Basic wavelength-related sensory encoding is not the goal-management and habit-overriding demand specified for executive control.
Binocular comparison is a perceptual depth operation, rather than a decision about which task goal should control behavior.
Proximity grouping is a form-perception principle and does not by itself require replacing a rule or overcoming a habit.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Exam 1 Review, slides 26–27: executive control, goals, priorities, and habits.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes why highly practiced behavior can be both useful and troublesome?
choices: Practice makes the response slower and more effortful but eliminates errors.
Practice can reduce attention demands, yet a learned response may intrude when the current goal changes.
Automatic responses are defined by their ability to follow any new rule without control.
Once behavior is practiced, difficulty and competing tasks no longer matter.
questions.explanation: Practice can support fast, relatively low-effort processing. That efficiency is not the same as flexibility: an established response may persist when a new goal requires inhibition or control.
choiceExplanations: The usual practice benefit is reduced demand or improved efficiency, and practice does not guarantee elimination of every error.
Reduced attention demand can aid routine performance while the same strong habit creates conflict after a goal or rule change.
Following arbitrary new rules is a reason controlled processing is valuable; automatic habits are not necessarily immediately flexible.
Practice reduces some demands but does not abolish all limits imposed by task difficulty or shared processing resources.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 10: automatic versus controlled processes; 105 Exam 1 Review, slides 27–28.

questions.prompt: A visual tracking task is paired either with another demanding visual task or with an equally difficult auditory task. Practice and response demands are matched. Under modality-specific resource accounts, which comparison is predicted?
choices: The auditory pairing must be impossible because the senses differ.
Both pairings must have identical costs because task similarity is irrelevant.
The visual pairing should generally create more competition for shared visual resources.
The visual pairing must be easier because both tasks enter through the same modality.
questions.explanation: Tasks using similar modality-specific resources tend to interfere more. Matching difficulty, practice, and response demands makes the sensory-resource overlap a more informative comparison; cross-modal costs may still remain.
choiceExplanations: Different modalities can reduce overlap in specific resources; sensory difference does not make performing the tasks impossible.
Resource accounts that include modality-specific pools predict a role for similarity even when baseline difficulty is matched.
Two visual tasks compete more directly for visual processing resources than a visual-auditory pair with otherwise matched demands.
Sharing a modality can increase competition, so common visual input is not by itself a reason to expect easier dual-task performance.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 10; 105 Exam 1 Review, slides 25 and 28: modality-specific resources and task similarity.

questions.prompt: Before practice, a task takes 600 ms alone and 760 ms with a second task. After practice, it takes 450 ms alone and 610 ms with the second task. Accuracy is unchanged. What happened to its absolute dual-task cost?
choices: It fell by 150 ms because the dual-task response became 150 ms faster.
It disappeared because the practiced dual-task response is close to the original single-task response.
It increased from 160 ms to 610 ms.
It remained 160 ms even though both single- and dual-task responses became faster.
questions.explanation: Absolute dual-task cost is dual minus the task's own single-task baseline: 760 − 600 = 160 and 610 − 450 = 160 ms. Faster raw dual-task responses alone do not show reduced interference.
choiceExplanations: Both baselines improve by 150 ms; subtracting each condition's own single-task time shows that the interference cost is unchanged.
Comparing practiced dual-task performance with an unpracticed single-task baseline mixes practice and interference effects.
The 610 ms value is the full practiced dual-task response time, not its excess over the 450 ms single-task baseline.
Both subtractions yield 160 ms, so this example shows faster performance without a smaller absolute dual-task penalty.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 10: factors affecting dual-task performance. Numerical data are hypothetical.

questions.prompt: During a two-task experiment, instructions change from equal priority to prioritizing task A. A becomes faster, while B becomes slower and less accurate. What is the most cautious resource-based interpretation?
choices: Limited resources may have been reallocated toward A at B's expense.
The participant's total processing capacity must have increased.
Task B no longer shares any resource with task A.
Task A has become completely automatic solely because its priority increased.
questions.explanation: A benefit to one task accompanied by costs to another is consistent with reallocating limited resources. It does not by itself show more total capacity, complete independence, or acquired automaticity.
choiceExplanations: The opposite changes in performance fit a trade-off in how available resources are allocated after the priority instruction.
B's deterioration does not establish a gain in total capacity; A's improvement may simply reflect resources diverted from B.
A priority-driven trade-off is consistent with shared limitations rather than proof that the tasks use entirely separate resources.
An instruction changes goals, not necessarily practice history or automaticity; faster prioritized performance cannot establish automatic processing.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 10; 105 Exam 1 Review, slides 25–26: limited resources and executive priorities.

questions.prompt: After many trials sorting cards by color, a participant correctly repeats a new instruction to sort by number but repeatedly continues using color. Which account best fits the review's perseveration example?
choices: The participant must be unable to see the cards' numbers.
The old rule continues to control behavior despite knowledge of the new goal, suggesting difficulty overriding a habitual set.
Knowing the instruction guarantees that executive control is functioning perfectly.
The behavior shows that practice always improves switching to a new rule.
questions.explanation: Perseveration is persistence of a previously appropriate response or rule after circumstances change. Knowing the new instruction is not identical to successfully controlling behavior according to it.
choiceExplanations: The pattern does not establish a visual inability to detect numbers; difficulty abandoning the old rule is a distinct explanation.
Continuing the color rule despite the stated number goal matches a failure to disengage an old set and implement current control.
Verbal knowledge of a rule can coexist with difficulty applying it, so repeating instructions does not prove intact executive performance.
Practice can strengthen the old response and make switching harder; these errors do not show an unconditional switching benefit.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Exam 1 Review, slide 27: executive control and perseveration in card sorting.

questions.prompt: An auditory secondary task is made much harder while a practiced visual tracking task stays physically unchanged. Tracking accuracy declines. Why is this compatible with the course's resource account?
choices: Different sensory modalities prevent any shared control demands, so the result is impossible.
Practice guarantees that tracking needs absolutely no attention.
The harder secondary task may consume more shared control or response resources, leaving less available for tracking.
Increasing auditory difficulty necessarily damages the visual system.
questions.explanation: Modality-specific separation and practice can reduce interference without eliminating shared task-general requirements. Increasing difficulty can increase competition for those remaining resources.
choiceExplanations: Different modalities can still rely on common executive or response-selection processes, so cross-modal interference is possible.
Practice can lower attentional demands but does not establish complete freedom from shared resources under every condition.
A greater secondary-task demand can consume resources that the tracking task still needs, despite its practice and different modality.
A performance trade-off under competing task demands does not imply damage to the sensory system.
questions.sourceNote: 105 Study Guide, Module 10; 105 Exam 1 Review, slides 26 and 28: task-general resources, difficulty, and practice.

questions.prompt: Dual-task costs, each measured against its matching single-task baseline, are 180 ms before practice and 80 ms after practice for similar tasks; they are 70 ms and 50 ms for dissimilar tasks. Accuracy is stable. Which conclusion follows from these hypothetical data?
choices: Practice has the same effect on both pairs because the similar pair remains slower at both practice levels.
