MRI requires stillness, scanner tolerance, and safety screening; metal contraindications depend on the implant/material. fNIRS can be more portable and movement-tolerant with superficial coverage. Optode/electrode movement and physiological changes still contaminate signals, requiring careful design and analysis.
rubric: EEG can be used in children and is relatively inexpensive but movement/electrical artifacts matter.
MRI requires stillness, scanner tolerance, and safety screening; metal contraindications depend on the implant/material.
fNIRS can be more portable and movement-tolerant with superficial coverage.
Optode/electrode movement and physiological changes still contaminate signals, requiring careful design and analysis.
commonMistakes: Movement-tolerant is not artifact-free. Motion can alter electrode/optode contact or the measured physiology, while a child's ability to tolerate a scanner also limits what usable MRI data can be obtained.

questions.prompt: A scanner study finds greater signal during face judgments than rest. Give two reasons this is insufficient to identify a uniquely face-specific mechanism, then propose a better comparison.
questions.explanation: Rest differs in visual stimulation, attention, decision, and response demands. The region may respond to several non-face processes. Use a matched non-face object judgment/control with comparable difficulty and motor demands. Selectivity still indicates involvement rather than necessity; perturbation/lesion evidence addresses a different claim.
rubric: Rest differs in visual stimulation, attention, decision, and response demands.
The region may respond to several non-face processes.
Use a matched non-face object judgment/control with comparable difficulty and motor demands.
Selectivity still indicates involvement rather than necessity; perturbation/lesion evidence addresses a different claim.
commonMistakes: Face judgments and rest differ in more than face recognition. Visual input, attention, decisions, and motor responses must be matched before attributing a contrast specifically to face-related processing.

questions.prompt: Distinguish involvement, necessity, and sufficiency using a hypothetical cortical region R. Match each to appropriate evidence and a limit.
questions.explanation: Involvement: R's signal covaries with task performance/conditions. Necessity: disrupting R impairs the function under specified conditions, with controls. Sufficiency: activating an appropriate system can produce the relevant outcome under specified conditions; this is stronger/different than task activation. Neither a scan correlation nor a simple impairment establishes all three or proves R acts alone.
rubric: Involvement: R's signal covaries with task performance/conditions.
Necessity: disrupting R impairs the function under specified conditions, with controls.
Sufficiency: activating an appropriate system can produce the relevant outcome under specified conditions; this is stronger/different than task activation.
Neither a scan correlation nor a simple impairment establishes all three or proves R acts alone.
commonMistakes: Involvement, necessity, and sufficiency are not a ladder automatically completed by one scan. A region can covary with a task without being necessary, and an impairment does not prove that activating that region alone produces the function.

questions.prompt: Compare organic lesion studies and TMS in control of location/timing, reorganization, within-person comparisons, and generalizability.
questions.explanation: Organic lesions are acquired rather than experimentally assigned and vary in extent/location. Chronic lesions allow compensatory reorganization and secondary effects; TMS offers more immediate time-specific perturbation. TMS permits within-person site/time controls but has depth/spatial and stimulation-effect limitations. Both require cautious generalization because injury populations and experimental perturbations differ from ordinary intact processing.
rubric: Organic lesions are acquired rather than experimentally assigned and vary in extent/location.
Chronic lesions allow compensatory reorganization and secondary effects; TMS offers more immediate time-specific perturbation.
TMS permits within-person site/time controls but has depth/spatial and stimulation-effect limitations.
Both require cautious generalization because injury populations and experimental perturbations differ from ordinary intact processing.
commonMistakes: An organic lesion is acquired damage, not a randomly assigned laboratory intervention. TMS improves control of site and timing but has its own depth/network effects; neither approach automatically removes compensation or generalizability concerns.

questions.prompt: Why can high temporal resolution and high spatial resolution answer different questions? Construct an example requiring EEG and fMRI evidence, and explain why combining them still does not prove necessity.
questions.explanation: Temporal resolution concerns when changes occur; spatial resolution concerns where they can be distinguished. EEG could establish an early versus late condition difference. fMRI could identify candidate regions with corresponding task selectivity. Complementary correlations can constrain a mechanism but remain nonperturbational; a controlled lesion/TMS design is needed to test causal necessity/contribution.
rubric: Temporal resolution concerns when changes occur; spatial resolution concerns where they can be distinguished.
EEG could establish an early versus late condition difference.
fMRI could identify candidate regions with corresponding task selectivity.
Complementary correlations can constrain a mechanism but remain nonperturbational; a controlled lesion/TMS design is needed to test causal necessity/contribution.
commonMistakes: Combining two correlations does not turn them into an intervention. Complementary where/when evidence narrows candidate mechanisms, but causal dependence still needs an appropriate perturbation or lesion argument with controls.

questions.prompt: Design a study to test a superficial region's contribution to face discrimination while measuring timing. Specify measurement, perturbation, control task, and a confound.
questions.explanation: Use EEG/ERP or timed behavioral effects to motivate a processing interval. Apply TMS to the accessible candidate site at that versus control times. Include matched object discrimination and sham/control-site conditions. Check eye movements, stimulation sensation, basic visibility, response demands, and speed-accuracy trade-offs; selective impairment supports a causal role under those conditions.
rubric: Use EEG/ERP or timed behavioral effects to motivate a processing interval.
Apply TMS to the accessible candidate site at that versus control times.
Include matched object discrimination and sham/control-site conditions.
Check eye movements, stimulation sensation, basic visibility, response demands, and speed-accuracy trade-offs; selective impairment supports a causal role under those conditions.
commonMistakes: A drop on every task could reflect distraction or motor effects rather than a selective face contribution. Match control-task demands and compare stimulation sites/times, while measuring both accuracy and speed.

questions.prompt: Define a strict grandmother-cell hypothesis. State what observations would be needed to establish its strongest version and why a selective recording falls short.
questions.explanation: The strongest hypothesis assigns one concept to one unique neuron that responds only to that concept. It requires exclusivity across alternatives and uniqueness across the relevant population. A selective response to tested examples cannot rule out untested preferred concepts or other cells carrying the same information. Necessity of that unique cell would require causal evidence; recording alone provides selectivity, not sole storage.
rubric: The strongest hypothesis assigns one concept to one unique neuron that responds only to that concept.
It requires exclusivity across alternatives and uniqueness across the relevant population.
A selective response to tested examples cannot rule out untested preferred concepts or other cells carrying the same information.
Necessity of that unique cell would require causal evidence; recording alone provides selectivity, not sole storage.
commonMistakes: A selective response to the tested actor images does not establish uniqueness across all neurons or exclusivity across all possible stimuli. Recording also does not show that destroying this cell would erase that concept.

questions.prompt: Compare local, sparse, and fully distributed coding using the same hypothetical 100-neuron population. State what changes when the represented concept changes.
questions.explanation: Local: one unit identifies a concept in the strict example. Sparse: a small subset, such as several of the 100, carries the pattern. Fully distributed: representation depends on activity spread across most/all units. Different concepts have different units/subsets or population activity patterns; code type concerns patterns, not merely the total number of neurons in the brain.
rubric: Local: one unit identifies a concept in the strict example.
Sparse: a small subset, such as several of the 100, carries the pattern.
Fully distributed: representation depends on activity spread across most/all units.
Different concepts have different units/subsets or population activity patterns; code type concerns patterns, not merely the total number of neurons in the brain.
commonMistakes: Sparse does not mean only a few neurons exist in the brain, and distributed does not require equal firing everywhere. The distinction concerns how a concept is represented across a defined population and how its pattern changes across concepts.

questions.prompt: Give four reasons the review favors sparse distributed representations over a literal one-cell-per-concept account. Include a qualification about energy claims.
questions.explanation: Overlapping combinations can support large representational capacity. Loss of one contributing cell need not erase the entire concept. Shared/overlapping features support generalization, categorization, and learning flexibility. Activating a small subset can be metabolically economical compared with widespread activation, but this is a conceptual argument rather than direct energy measurement in the reviewed experiments.
rubric: Overlapping combinations can support large representational capacity.
Loss of one contributing cell need not erase the entire concept.
Shared/overlapping features support generalization, categorization, and learning flexibility.
Activating a small subset can be metabolically economical compared with widespread activation, but this is a conceptual argument rather than direct energy measurement in the reviewed experiments.
commonMistakes: These advantages motivate sparse representations but are not all directly measured by the reviewed experiments. In particular, a conceptual energy-efficiency argument must not be reported as if the studies measured metabolic savings.

questions.prompt: A neuron responds to several photographs of one actor but not to 40 tested distractors. Distinguish selectivity from invariance and give two unjustified conclusions.
questions.explanation: Selectivity is preferential responding to some concepts/stimuli over tested alternatives. Invariance is consistent responding across changes in visual examples of the same identity. It is unjustified to infer no untested concept could activate it. It is unjustified to infer it is the only/necessary cell representing that actor.
rubric: Selectivity is preferential responding to some concepts/stimuli over tested alternatives.
Invariance is consistent responding across changes in visual examples of the same identity.
It is unjustified to infer no untested concept could activate it.
It is unjustified to infer it is the only/necessary cell representing that actor.
commonMistakes: Selectivity compares the actor with tested alternatives; invariance compares different images of the same actor. Neither comparison proves how the cell responds to every untested concept or how many other cells carry the actor's identity.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct the Quiroga study's question, participants/access, stimulus procedure, and recorded measure. State which parts make it a rare human neural opportunity.
questions.explanation: Ask whether human medial temporal neurons show selective, invariant responses to high-level visual concepts. Use epilepsy patients with clinically implanted depth electrodes; the review describes eight patients. Present varied images of faces, landmarks, objects, and animals in controlled/pseudorandom order, about one second each in the review. Record single-unit firing; clinical access permits invasive human sampling unavailable in ordinary healthy volunteers.
rubric: Ask whether human medial temporal neurons show selective, invariant responses to high-level visual concepts.
Use epilepsy patients with clinically implanted depth electrodes; the review describes eight patients.
Present varied images of faces, landmarks, objects, and animals in controlled/pseudorandom order, about one second each in the review.
Record single-unit firing; clinical access permits invasive human sampling unavailable in ordinary healthy volunteers.
commonMistakes: Do not substitute scalp EEG, healthy volunteers, or marmosets for the reviewed Quiroga design. The opportunity came from clinical intracranial access in human epilepsy patients, with electrode placement constrained by clinical needs.

questions.prompt: Explain the main Quiroga result and why it supports abstract/selective coding without proving a literal grandmother cell. Include two generalizability limitations.
questions.explanation: Some cells respond preferentially to a concept across different images. Some respond to more than one stimulus/concept, consistent with sparse coding rather than strict exclusivity. Epilepsy patients and clinically determined electrode sites are selective samples. Limited tested stimuli/neurons and correlational recording constrain exclusivity, population, and necessity claims.
rubric: Some cells respond preferentially to a concept across different images.
Some respond to more than one stimulus/concept, consistent with sparse coding rather than strict exclusivity.
Epilepsy patients and clinically determined electrode sites are selective samples.
Limited tested stimuli/neurons and correlational recording constrain exclusivity, population, and necessity claims.
commonMistakes: Finding abstract or invariant responses is stronger than finding nothing, but weaker than proving a unique grandmother cell. Limited stimuli, recorded neurons, clinical participants, and electrode sites restrict exclusivity and generalization claims.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct the Tyree study's species/region, modalities, recording approach, and principal question.
questions.explanation: The review describes four marmosets with hippocampal recordings. Stimuli include other individuals' faces, voices, and audiovisual combinations. Analyses examine single-neuron responses and population activity. The question is whether identity is represented across sensory modalities rather than only through one particular image or sound.
rubric: The review describes four marmosets with hippocampal recordings.
Stimuli include other individuals' faces, voices, and audiovisual combinations.
Analyses examine single-neuron responses and population activity.
The question is whether identity is represented across sensory modalities rather than only through one particular image or sound.
commonMistakes: Do not confuse the species and modality manipulation with Quiroga's human visual-image study. The reviewed Tyree design used marmoset hippocampal recordings with faces, voices, and audiovisual presentations to examine identity across modalities.

questions.prompt: What results would distinguish identity coding from separate face-only and voice-only responses? Explain the reviewed Tyree findings at single-cell and population levels and one inference limit.
questions.explanation: An identity-sensitive cell/pattern should distinguish individuals and generalize across their face/voice presentations. The review reports a subset of neurons with cross-modal identity responses, roughly 9% in its summary. Population activity also contains identity information. These results support cross-modal representations but do not prove one exclusive necessary cell or that all neurons respond identically.
rubric: An identity-sensitive cell/pattern should distinguish individuals and generalize across their face/voice presentations.
The review reports a subset of neurons with cross-modal identity responses, roughly 9% in its summary.
Population activity also contains identity information.
These results support cross-modal representations but do not prove one exclusive necessary cell or that all neurons respond identically.
commonMistakes: Separate face and voice responses do not automatically show that the same identity code generalizes across them. The review's approximate 9% is a subset estimate, not a claim that every hippocampal neuron responds identically or is necessary for recognition.

questions.prompt: Compare Quiroga and Tyree on species, modality manipulation, neural access/region, and the strongest shared conclusion.
questions.explanation: Quiroga: humans with epilepsy; Tyree: marmosets. Reviewed Quiroga evidence emphasizes invariance across visual images; Tyree explicitly compares face/voice modalities. Both use invasive single-neuron evidence in medial-temporal/hippocampal systems, with population analysis emphasized for Tyree. Both support selective high-level identity/concept representations compatible with sparse/population coding; neither establishes sole-cell necessity.
rubric: Quiroga: humans with epilepsy; Tyree: marmosets.
Reviewed Quiroga evidence emphasizes invariance across visual images; Tyree explicitly compares face/voice modalities.
Both use invasive single-neuron evidence in medial-temporal/hippocampal systems, with population analysis emphasized for Tyree.
Both support selective high-level identity/concept representations compatible with sparse/population coding; neither establishes sole-cell necessity.
commonMistakes: The studies are not identical replications: human clinical visual-image invariance and marmoset cross-modal identity address different manipulations. Their shared selectivity evidence remains compatible with sparse/population coding rather than unique-cell necessity.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical population distinguishes two individuals from face trials and can also distinguish them from voice trials. What extra test would strengthen a shared cross-modal-code claim? Explain why successful decoding is not proof of necessity.
questions.explanation: Train a classifier on faces and test on held-out voices, or reverse, while controlling identity labels and confounds. Above-chance cross-modal generalization supports a shared identity-related pattern more strongly than two separate within-modality results. Use held-out data and controls for stimulus familiarity/task/motor effects. Decodability means information is present in measured activity, not that this population is uniquely used or necessary for behavior. This is an application extension, not a claim about every analysis in Tyree.
rubric: Train a classifier on faces and test on held-out voices, or reverse, while controlling identity labels and confounds.
Above-chance cross-modal generalization supports a shared identity-related pattern more strongly than two separate within-modality results.
Use held-out data and controls for stimulus familiarity/task/motor effects.

Decodability means information is present in measured activity, not that this population is uniquely used or necessary for behavior. This is an application extension, not a claim about every analysis in Tyree.
commonMistakes: Success on separate face-only and voice-only classifiers does not by itself demonstrate a shared cross-modal pattern. Cross-modal testing must use held-out data; even successful decoding shows available information, not unique behavioral necessity.

questions.prompt: Define a single dissociation. Use a shared-resource model to explain a patient impaired on a hard task but spared on an easy task without assuming different modules.
questions.explanation: A single dissociation is impairment on one task with relative preservation on another. Suppose both require the same resource. The harder task requires more of it and falls below its performance threshold after damage. The easier task remains above threshold; this is a task-resource/difficulty explanation rather than evidence compelling separate systems.
rubric: A single dissociation is impairment on one task with relative preservation on another.
Suppose both require the same resource.
The harder task requires more of it and falls below its performance threshold after damage.
The easier task remains above threshold; this is a task-resource/difficulty explanation rather than evidence compelling separate systems.
commonMistakes: A selective deficit on the harder task does not compel two separate modules. The same reduced resource can leave enough capacity for an easy task while the harder one falls below its requirement.

questions.prompt: Hypothetical controls score 95% on A and B. Patient X scores A 35/B 92; patient Y scores A 90/B 30. Explain the pattern, the simple account it challenges, and the limit of the inference.
questions.explanation: X has selective A impairment and Y selective B impairment. This is a double dissociation. A single fixed resource with one task always more demanding cannot readily explain both opposite patterns. It supports differentiated resources but not complete independence; measure reliability, task comparability, and lesion/network differences matter.
rubric: X has selective A impairment and Y selective B impairment.
This is a double dissociation.
A single fixed resource with one task always more demanding cannot readily explain both opposite patterns.
It supports differentiated resources but not complete independence; measure reliability, task comparability, and lesion/network differences matter.
commonMistakes: Opposite selective deficits challenge a simple shared resource with one fixed difficulty ordering. They do not imply that the tasks never share any processing or that lesion extent and measurement reliability can be ignored.

questions.prompt: Why is comparing a patient's two raw percentages insufficient by itself to establish a selective deficit? Specify relevant controls and a stronger performance comparison.
questions.explanation: Tasks can differ in baseline difficulty, chance level, and measurement scale. Use control participants and relevant norms/single-task baselines. Establish whether impairment relative to the appropriate baseline differs across tasks, with uncertainty/reliability considered. Preserve comparable sensory/motor demands and enough trials to avoid mistaking noisy or ceiling/floor data for a dissociation.
rubric: Tasks can differ in baseline difficulty, chance level, and measurement scale.
Use control participants and relevant norms/single-task baselines.
Establish whether impairment relative to the appropriate baseline differs across tasks, with uncertainty/reliability considered.
Preserve comparable sensory/motor demands and enough trials to avoid mistaking noisy or ceiling/floor data for a dissociation.
commonMistakes: Raw percentages can have different baselines, chance levels, and reliabilities. Compare each task with suitable controls before interpreting a difference as selective impairment rather than unequal difficulty or measurement noise.

questions.prompt: Give four considerations that limit generalization from a single lesion patient. Explain how each could alter the observed task result.
questions.explanation: Unknown pre-injury abilities can make a deficit/preservation hard to interpret. Individual anatomy and lesion extent/location can differ from typical brains. Time since injury allows reorganization/compensation. Secondary effects such as depression, fatigue, medication, or broader impairment can affect performance. A single case can still strongly constrain a universal theory.
rubric: Unknown pre-injury abilities can make a deficit/preservation hard to interpret.
Individual anatomy and lesion extent/location can differ from typical brains.
Time since injury allows reorganization/compensation.
Secondary effects such as depression, fatigue, medication, or broader impairment can affect performance. A single case can still strongly constrain a universal theory.
commonMistakes: A post-injury score is not a direct measure of lost ability when the pre-injury baseline is unknown. Lesion extent, compensation, fatigue, and other secondary effects can also change performance without mapping neatly onto one isolated function.

questions.prompt: Distinguish a crossed fMRI preference pattern from a lesion double dissociation. Why is calling both 'double dissociation' not permission to make identical causal claims?
questions.explanation: A crossed activation pattern shows different relative condition preferences in measured signals. A lesion double dissociation shows opposite selective behavioral impairments following damage. The first primarily supports differentiated involvement; the second provides evidence about causal dependence with lesion confounds. Neither alone establishes exclusive isolated modules; the evidence types and controls differ.
rubric: A crossed activation pattern shows different relative condition preferences in measured signals.
A lesion double dissociation shows opposite selective behavioral impairments following damage.
The first primarily supports differentiated involvement; the second provides evidence about causal dependence with lesion confounds.
Neither alone establishes exclusive isolated modules; the evidence types and controls differ.
commonMistakes: A crossed activation preference does not disrupt anything, whereas lesion evidence concerns performance after damage. Sharing the phrase "double dissociation" does not give an activation contrast the same causal force as a controlled impairment argument.

questions.prompt: An article claims: 'Two lesion patients prove faces and objects are processed in completely separate modules, and an actor-selective neuron proves a unique grandmother cell.' Repair both claims and propose one follow-up for each.
questions.explanation: Opposite lesion deficits support partially differentiated resources, not complete independence. A follow-up can match task difficulty/sensory demands and examine additional patients or controlled perturbations. Actor selectivity/invariance is consistent with participation in a sparse ensemble, not unique exclusive storage. A follow-up can test more stimuli/neurons and population generalization or a justified causal intervention. State evidence limits rather than replacing all conclusions with 'nothing is known.'
rubric: Opposite lesion deficits support partially differentiated resources, not complete independence.
A follow-up can match task difficulty/sensory demands and examine additional patients or controlled perturbations.
Actor selectivity/invariance is consistent with participation in a sparse ensemble, not unique exclusive storage.
A follow-up can test more stimuli/neurons and population generalization or a justified causal intervention. State evidence limits rather than replacing all conclusions with 'nothing is known.'
commonMistakes: Avoid both overclaiming and dismissing the evidence entirely. Double dissociations constrain shared-resource accounts, and selective cells constrain coding accounts, but stronger claims of complete independence or unique storage need additional targeted tests.

questions.prompt: A researcher divides cortex into areas after inspecting neuron shapes and the arrangement of cells in tissue sections. Which organizing principle is being used?
choices: Cytoarchitecture
Surface folding
Functional responses
Connectivity
questions.explanation: Cytoarchitecture groups cortical areas by their cellular structure, including cell types and their arrangement; Brodmann areas are the course example.
choiceExplanations: Cytoarchitecture groups cortical areas by their cellular structure, including cell types and their arrangement; Brodmann areas are the course example.
Surface folding concerns visible gyri and sulci, whereas this researcher is using microscopic cellular organization to set boundaries.
Functional grouping would require evidence about what information neurons respond to or what operations an area supports, not cell appearance alone.
Connectivity classifies areas through their inputs and outputs; inspecting cell shapes without tracing connections does not provide that evidence.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Study Guide: Neuroanatomy; PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Review, page 8.

questions.prompt: On a cortical surface, a probe moves from the crest of a fold down into the adjacent groove. What has it moved from and into?
choices: White matter into a basal ganglion
A gyrus into a sulcus
A sulcus into a gyrus
A cortical column into a ventricle
questions.explanation: A gyrus is a raised cortical fold and a sulcus is a groove between folds; these terms describe the surface geometry.
choiceExplanations: Surface folds are formed by cortex; a crease in that surface is not a transition from an axon bundle into a deep nucleus.
A gyrus is a raised cortical fold and a sulcus is a groove between folds; these terms describe the surface geometry.
This reverses the terms: the probe starts on a raised gyrus and ends in a recessed sulcus.
Columns concern cortical organization, and ventricles are internal CSF-filled spaces; neither term names the crest-to-groove transition.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Study Guide: Neuroanatomy; PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Review, page 7.

questions.prompt: Which description correctly separates two different forms of neocortical organization?
choices: Layers are white-matter bundles; columns are fluid-filled spaces.
Each fold is one layer; each hemisphere is one column.
Layers partition cortical thickness; columns extend across layers.
Layers are lobes; columns are the grooves separating them.
questions.explanation: Neocortex has six layers arranged across its thickness, while cortical columns are functional groupings oriented through those layers.
choiceExplanations: Layers and columns both describe cortical organization; white-matter bundles and ventricles are different anatomical categories.
A folded patch still contains multiple cortical layers and many columns; macroscopic folding does not define a single layer or column.
Neocortex has six layers arranged across its thickness, while cortical columns are functional groupings oriented through those layers.
Cortical layers are microscopic divisions across cortical thickness, not lobes, and columns are not surface sulci.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Study Guide: Neuroanatomy; PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Review, page 7.

questions.prompt: Two samples are described: A contains many neuronal cell bodies and synapses; B contains many myelinated axons. Which classification best matches their dominant contents?
choices: A is white matter; B is gray matter.
A is CSF; B is a ventricle.
Both must be cortex because all neural tissue is cortical.
A is gray matter; B is white matter.
questions.explanation: Gray matter is rich in cell bodies and synapses, whereas white matter is rich in myelinated axons carrying signals between locations.
choiceExplanations: This reverses the main tissue distinction: myelinated axons characterize white matter more than the cell-body-rich sample does.
CSF is fluid and a ventricle is a fluid-filled space; neither is a tissue class defined by abundant neurons or myelinated axons.
Neural tissue also includes deep nuclei and connecting pathways; a sample containing neurons or axons need not come from cortex.
Gray matter is rich in cell bodies and synapses, whereas white matter is rich in myelinated axons carrying signals between locations.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Study Guide: Neuroanatomy; PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Review, page 9.

questions.prompt: Which observation would most directly justify calling a cortical white-matter pathway commissural?
choices: Its cortical endpoints lie in opposite hemispheres.
Its cortical endpoints lie far apart within one hemisphere.
It carries signals from cortex toward the spinal cord.
It contains many axons surrounded by myelin.
questions.explanation: Commissural pathways connect across the hemispheres; the corpus callosum is the major example emphasized in the course.
choiceExplanations: Commissural pathways connect across the hemispheres; the corpus callosum is the major example emphasized in the course.
Distance alone does not make a pathway commissural; a long cortex-to-cortex connection within one hemisphere is association.
A cortex-to-lower-CNS connection is classified as projection rather than by the commissural criterion of linking the hemispheres.
Myelinated axons occur in all three tract classes; myelin identifies white-matter composition, not the commissural endpoint pattern.

questions.prompt: Which statement captures the projection-fiber category without confusing it with a direction of information flow?
choices: It is any pathway visible in a projected brain image.
It links cortex with noncortical CNS structures.
It includes only descending fibers from cortex.
It links two cortical areas within the same hemisphere.
questions.explanation: Projection pathways link cortical and noncortical CNS levels; the category includes connections carrying information toward cortex as well as away from it.
choiceExplanations: The word projection here names an anatomical tract class, not an image-rendering technique or the visibility of a pathway in a picture.
Projection pathways link cortical and noncortical CNS levels; the category includes connections carrying information toward cortex as well as away from it.
Descending pathways such as the corticospinal tract are examples, but projection is a connectivity class rather than a synonym for descending.
Two cortical endpoints within one hemisphere define association connections, not projection pathways.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Study Guide: Neuroanatomy; PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Review, page 10.

questions.prompt: Which set contains three basal ganglia components named in the review?
choices: Thalamus, hypothalamus, and cerebellum
Corpus callosum, superior longitudinal fasciculus, and corticospinal tract
Caudate, putamen, and globus pallidus
Hippocampus, amygdala, and olfactory bulb
questions.explanation: The review names the caudate nucleus, putamen, and globus pallidus as components of the basal ganglia located deep in the brain.
choiceExplanations: These are important structures with distinct roles, but they are not the three basal ganglia components specified in the review.
These examples are white-matter pathways rather than the deep gray-matter structures making up the named basal ganglia set.
The review names the caudate nucleus, putamen, and globus pallidus as components of the basal ganglia located deep in the brain.

questions.prompt: A student sees a brain diagram with several connected spaces filled with CSF. What category do those spaces belong to?
choices: Cortical columns
Commissural tracts
Basal ganglia nuclei
Ventricles
questions.explanation: Ventricles are spaces containing cerebrospinal fluid; they should not be mistaken for solid nuclei or bundles of axons.

Commissural tracts are axon pathways linking the hemispheres, not cavities whose defining contents are CSF.
Basal ganglia nuclei are collections of neural tissue deep in the brain, not interconnected fluid-filled ventricular spaces.
Ventricles are spaces containing cerebrospinal fluid; they should not be mistaken for solid nuclei or bundles of axons.

questions.prompt: Which pairing best matches the broad hippocampus/amygdala distinction emphasized in the study guide?
choices: Hippocampus: learning and memory; amygdala: threat and emotional significance.
Hippocampus: endocrine regulation; amygdala: primary sensory relay to cortex.
Hippocampus: CSF-filled cavity; amygdala: myelinated interhemispheric bundle.
Hippocampus: muscle force production; amygdala: formation of myelin sheaths.
questions.explanation: These are the broad associations in the supplied materials, while neither structure is the sole location of all memory or all emotion.

questions.prompt: Which two neighboring structures are grouped under the diencephalon in the review?
choices: Cerebrum and cerebellum
Thalamus and hypothalamus
Caudate and putamen
Hippocampus and amygdala

questions.prompt: Which operation best matches the cerebellar role emphasized in the review?
choices: Cushioning the brain with ventricular fluid
Connecting the cerebral hemispheres as a major axon bundle
Coordinating movement using sensory feedback
Linking nervous and endocrine regulation

questions.prompt: Investigators find that neurons responding strongly to the same type of visual information are clustered together. They use this response pattern to define an area. Which classification are they using?
choices: Cytoarchitecture alone
Surface folding alone
A ventricular classification
Functional organization

The investigators did not locate the group by the geometry of gyri or sulci; their defining evidence is the neurons' response pattern.

questions.prompt: Two cortical areas contain similar-looking cells, but one receives visual inputs and the other receives different sensory inputs. Why might the areas contribute differently to behavior?
choices: Different inputs and outputs can support different functions.
Similar cells guarantee identical functions despite different inputs.
Sensory inputs make both regions white-matter tracts.
Functional differences imply that one area lacks neurons.
questions.explanation: The review emphasizes that inputs and outputs matter for function; similar cytoarchitecture alone does not establish equivalent processing roles.
choiceExplanations: The review emphasizes that inputs and outputs matter for function; similar cytoarchitecture alone does not establish equivalent processing roles.

questions.prompt: A classmate labels every deep brain structure as white matter because it lies beneath the cortex. Which observation most directly corrects that rule?
choices: Myelinated axons can be classified only at the surface.
Cell-rich deep nuclei are gray matter too.
All structures below cortex contain only CSF.
Connections make cortex a form of white matter.

Ventricles contain CSF, but deep brain anatomy also includes nuclei and pathways; depth does not imply a fluid-filled space.

questions.prompt: Two neighboring gyri in the left hemisphere communicate through a short cortex-to-cortex bundle. Why is it still an association connection?
choices: Association fibers require a minimum long-range distance.
A short connection must be a ventricle rather than a tract.
Same-hemisphere cortical endpoints define the class.
Crossing a sulcus makes the tract commissural.

Ventricles are CSF-filled spaces; tract length does not turn a neural connection into a fluid-filled cavity.

questions.prompt: A traced pathway links left frontal cortex to right parietal cortex. A student rejects the commissural label because the two endpoints are in different lobes. What is the best correction?
choices: Different lobe names make any pathway association.

The causal question concerns task performance; removing behavioral evidence would not distinguish neural disruption from distracting side effects.

questions.sourceNote: PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Study Guide: Comparison of methods (signal origin, resolution, setup, invasiveness, and necessity versus involvement); PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Review, page 25.

questions.prompt: A participant cannot safely enter the MRI scanner under the study's screening criteria. The main remaining goal is noninvasive timing of responses to brief sounds. Which adjustment best fits that goal?
choices: Infer trial-by-trial timing from one structural brain image
Use fNIRS to resolve event ordering at single-millisecond precision
Consider EEG with appropriate screening and recording procedures
Keep MRI because all noninvasive methods lack contraindications
questions.explanation: EEG can measure millisecond-scale event-related electrical responses outside an MRI scanner, matching the timing goal if suitable for the participant and protocol.
choiceExplanations: A structural anatomical image does not contain the trial-specific electrical timing information required by this goal.
fNIRS is noninvasive but relies on slower hemoglobin changes; it does not replace EEG's electrical temporal resolution for this question.
EEG can measure millisecond-scale event-related electrical responses outside an MRI scanner, matching the timing goal if suitable for the participant and protocol.
Noninvasive does not mean free of contraindications; the review specifically notes scanner-related restrictions and practical requirements.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Study Guide: Comparison of methods (signal origin, resolution, setup, invasiveness, and necessity versus involvement); PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Review, page 21.

questions.prompt: A scanner samples BOLD data very frequently. A report claims that the time series therefore gives the exact order of neural events separated by 20 ms. What is the key error?
choices: Sub-20 ms sampling alone would establish the claim.
Smaller voxels alone would resolve the event order.
Trial averaging removes the biological delay and recovers exact spikes.
Sampling faster does not speed up the blood response.
questions.explanation: The acquisition interval and the biological speed of the measured response are different; frequent BOLD samples do not directly resolve the exact order of neural events 20 ms apart.
choiceExplanations: A smaller acquisition interval does not eliminate the blood response's slow relationship to neural events; sampling rate alone cannot resolve the inference.
Spatial precision and temporal inference are different limits; smaller voxels do not turn the hemodynamic signal into a direct millisecond neural record.
Averaging can improve signal-to-noise but does not remove the biological transformation from neural activity to blood-related contrast or recover exact spike timing by itself.
The acquisition interval and the biological speed of the measured response are different; frequent BOLD samples do not directly resolve the exact order of neural events 20 ms apart.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Study Guide: Comparison of methods (signal origin, resolution, setup, invasiveness, and necessity versus involvement); PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Review, pages 22.

questions.prompt: An EEG study detects a task effect near 200 ms, and a separate fMRI study localizes a response during the same task. Which combined conclusion goes beyond the evidence?
choices: The fMRI-localized region is the unique generator of the 200 ms effect.
EEG constrains when some task-related electrical processing differs.
fMRI identifies a region with a task-related physiological response.
The results can guide a perturbation test of location and timing.
questions.explanation: Sharing a task does not establish a unique link between an EEG component and a particular fMRI-localized region; complementary observations need additional source-linking evidence.
choiceExplanations: Sharing a task does not establish a unique link between an EEG component and a particular fMRI-localized region; complementary observations need additional source-linking evidence.
A reliably event-locked EEG effect can provide temporal constraints on processing, even when its contributing neural sources remain uncertain.
A properly analyzed fMRI contrast supports this involvement claim without identifying the unique generator of a particular scalp electrical component.
Complementary localization and timing results can motivate a causal follow-up; using them to design a test is weaker than assuming the causal link is already proved.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Study Guide: Comparison of methods (signal origin, resolution, setup, invasiveness, and necessity versus involvement); PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Review, pages 19,22.

questions.prompt: A well-powered fNIRS experiment finds no condition difference at its scalp sensors. The authors conclude that the hippocampus responded equally to both conditions. Which objection is decisive?
choices: Matched behavioral performance establishes equal hippocampal responses.
More statistical power does not overcome limited depth coverage.
More participants at the same sites would establish the deep-region null.
A reliable control-task signal would validate hippocampal coverage.
questions.explanation: Conventional fNIRS samples superficial hemodynamic responses; precise estimates at scalp sensors do not provide a direct estimate of a deep hippocampal condition difference.
choiceExplanations: Similar behavior can arise from different neural processing; behavioral equivalence does not establish equal hippocampal activity beyond the method's depth coverage.
Conventional fNIRS samples superficial hemodynamic responses; precise estimates at scalp sensors do not provide a direct estimate of a deep hippocampal condition difference.
Additional participants can improve sensitivity for the measured signal, but they cannot give a superficial optical setup direct access to an unsampled deep structure.
A control response can show that the sensors detect some signal, but it does not establish that the detected source is the hippocampus.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Study Guide: Comparison of methods (signal origin, resolution, setup, invasiveness, and necessity versus involvement); PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Review, pages 23.

questions.prompt: Single-unit recordings accurately measure responses in a few brain locations selected for clinical reasons. Which extension of the experiment best addresses a limitation that collecting more trials from the same units would leave unresolved?
choices: Use finer time bins and interpret them as broader population sampling.
Average the units and interpret that average as a typical healthy brain.
Broaden regional and clinical sampling where ethical.
Add same-unit trials and interpret them as broader brain coverage.
questions.explanation: More trials improve estimates for sampled units, but broader sampling addresses whether those units and clinical locations represent the wider neural systems of interest.
choiceExplanations: Finer temporal analysis changes time resolution, not the number of regions or clinical contexts represented in the sample.
Averaging local clinical recordings does not make the sample representative of an entire healthy brain or eliminate differences among sampled neurons.
More trials improve estimates for sampled units, but broader sampling addresses whether those units and clinical locations represent the wider neural systems of interest.
Additional trials can improve reliability at existing recording sites; they do not add unsampled regions or remove clinical selection limits.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Study Guide: Comparison of methods (signal origin, resolution, setup, invasiveness, and necessity versus involvement); PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Review, pages 18.

questions.prompt: TMS produces no behavioral effect at one cortical target and one time window. Which next step best distinguishes a weak test from evidence against a contribution at that target?
choices: Precisely estimate the null at the same setting and infer irrelevance.
Use an fMRI response at the target as proof of necessity.
Infer the region is optional because a causal role must survive any protocol.
Validate targeting and test plausible timing with controls.
questions.explanation: A null effect can result from ineffective targeting or mistimed stimulation; examining these factors and controls makes the causal test more informative.
choiceExplanations: Precision at one possibly ineffective or mistimed setting does not establish that the region never contributes; validity of the perturbation must also be checked.
An fMRI response can suggest involvement and help choose a target, but it does not turn the null perturbation into evidence of necessity.
A region can contribute even when one protocol fails to disrupt it sufficiently; a null result does not by itself establish optionality or successful compensation.
A null effect can result from ineffective targeting or mistimed stimulation; examining these factors and controls makes the causal test more informative.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Study Guide: Comparison of methods (signal origin, resolution, setup, invasiveness, and necessity versus involvement); PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Review, pages 25.

questions.prompt: EEG and fMRI both show a larger response in task A than task B. Which account best preserves both their physical differences and their shared inferential limit?
choices: Electrical and blood-related responses converge on involvement, not necessity.
Both count spikes, so agreement identifies the same generating neurons.
Both support involvement, and convergence is equivalent to perturbation.
The electrical measure establishes necessity; only fMRI is observational.
questions.explanation: EEG measures electrical population activity while BOLD fMRI measures a blood-related physiological response; agreement can strengthen involvement evidence without establishing a necessary causal contribution.
choiceExplanations: EEG measures electrical population activity while BOLD fMRI measures a blood-related physiological response; agreement can strengthen involvement evidence without establishing a necessary causal contribution.
Scalp EEG is dominated by summed postsynaptic activity and BOLD is indirect; matching condition effects do not identify the same individual neurons.
Converging observation is useful but is not equivalent to altering a region's contribution and measuring the resulting change in performance.
A direct electrical measurement remains observational; being closer to neural activity does not by itself establish what is necessary for the task.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Study Guide: Comparison of methods (signal origin, resolution, setup, invasiveness, and necessity versus involvement); PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Review, pages 19,22.

questions.prompt: In the grandmother-cell thought experiment, what makes the proposed neuron a 'grandmother cell' rather than merely a visually responsive cell?
choices: It responds to every face because all faces share visual features.
It is assigned to a highly specific, complex concept such as one's grandmother.
It responds only when every other neuron in its population also responds.
It has a larger action potential than neurons coding unfamiliar people.
questions.explanation: The thought experiment concerns representational specificity: a single unit stands for a complex concept. It is not defined by spike size or by generic face responsiveness.
choiceExplanations: A response to every face would indicate broad face sensitivity, not the highly specific concept assignment in the grandmother-cell proposal.
The proposed cell stands for a particular complex entity. That highly specific assignment is what makes this a local representation thought experiment.
Requiring the entire population to respond describes a population-wide pattern, not the proposed single-cell assignment of one complex concept.
The coding distinction concerns which neurons respond to which concepts. A uniquely larger spike is not part of the grandmother-cell hypothesis.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Review, slides 29–30; Study Guide: grandmother-cell thought experiment and coding theories.

questions.prompt: Which phrase correctly completes the definition of sparse coding: 'A concept is represented by activity in…'?
choices: a small subset of the relevant population, potentially overlapping with subsets for other concepts.
exactly one indispensable neuron, with no other neuron carrying information about that concept.
the same uniform response in every neuron, regardless of which concept is presented.
all neurons throughout the nervous system rather than a defined neural population.
questions.explanation: Sparse coding uses a small portion of a population. Overlapping subsets can represent different concepts without requiring one unique storage neuron per concept.
choiceExplanations: A limited active subset is the defining feature of sparse coding. Different concepts may recruit partly overlapping subsets of the same population.
One unique, indispensable concept neuron is the strict local account. Sparse coding permits multiple contributing neurons for a concept.
An identical response to all concepts would not distinguish them. Sparse coding concerns selective activity patterns, not uniform population firing.
Coding density is defined relative to a relevant population. Sparse coding does not require a signal to involve every neuron in the nervous system.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Review, slides 29–30; Study Guide: local, sparse, and fully distributed representations.

questions.prompt: A diagram labels a representation 'fully distributed.' In the review's comparison, what should that label tell you?
choices: The concept is represented only by the anatomically largest neuron.
The concept has no representation because no single cell is sufficient.
Only a tiny fraction of the defined population participates in the code.
The representation is spread across activity throughout the defined population.
questions.explanation: Fully distributed representation spreads the code across the population. The label describes the breadth of participation, not the absence of information or the physical size of cells.
choiceExplanations: Cell size is not the criterion separating these coding theories. A single-cell assignment would instead be the local-coding extreme.
Information can reside in a population pattern even when no individual neuron is sufficient. Distribution does not mean that representation is absent.
Participation by only a small fraction describes sparse coding. Fully distributed coding is the broader-population endpoint in the review.
The review contrasts firing across a population with one-unit and small-subset accounts. The relevant unit of comparison is a defined population.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Review, slide 29; Study Guide: theories of neural representation.

questions.prompt: Why does losing a neuron pose a particularly sharp problem for the strict one-cell-per-concept thought experiment?
choices: The loss should affect only the visual appearance of the concept while leaving its identity fully stored in that same cell.
The concept should be preserved because the strict account already assumes an overlapping ensemble of other contributors.
If that cell alone carries the concept, its loss leaves no remaining representation of that concept.
The loss should damage every concept equally because the strict account assigns all concepts to the same population pattern.
questions.explanation: The critique follows from unique storage: removing the sole representative would remove the concept's only neural representation. Sparse ensembles can have surviving contributors.
choiceExplanations: The strict thought experiment assigns the complex concept itself to the cell. It does not separately guarantee a surviving identity representation after that cell is lost.
An overlapping ensemble would provide a distributed alternative, but it is not part of the strict unique-cell account whose fragility is being evaluated.
With no other contributing representation, losing the unique cell would erase the concept under the strict account. This motivates distributed alternatives.
Equal damage across all concepts is not predicted by a separate exclusive neuron for each concept. The sharp objection concerns the uniquely assigned concept.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Review, slide 30; Study Guide: arguments against grandmother cells.

questions.prompt: The review lists energy conservation as an argument for sparse coding. What is the relevant comparison?
choices: Activating a small subset can require less activity than activating a broad population for each concept.
The reviewed recordings directly measured the total metabolic cost of every concept.
Sparse coding is economical because fewer neurons must exist in the brain overall.
The energy argument establishes that a sparse code always uses less energy than a single active local unit.
questions.explanation: The argument is that limiting the active subset can be economical relative to widespread activation. It does not claim that sparse codes require no activity or that these studies directly measured energy use.
choiceExplanations: The proposed advantage follows from fewer simultaneously active contributors compared with a broad active population. It is a rationale, not an energy measurement here.
The review presents energy economy as an argument for sparse representations. It does not report direct measurements of the total metabolic cost of each concept.
Sparse describes the fraction active for a representation, not a requirement that the brain contain fewer neurons. Existing neurons can participate in different combinations.
The argument compares a small active subset with widespread activation. It does not by itself establish a universal energy advantage over every single-unit account.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Review, slide 30; Study Guide: arguments for sparse distributed representation.

questions.prompt: Which coding proposal most naturally allows two related concepts to share some contributing neurons while still having different representations?
choices: A strict account that assigns each entire concept to one exclusive neuron only.
An account in which every concept produces exactly the same activity pattern.
An account that forbids any neuron from contributing to more than one concept.
A sparse distributed account with overlapping but nonidentical active subsets.
questions.explanation: Overlapping subsets can capture commonality while differences between subsets distinguish the concepts. The review links sparse representation to generalization and categorization.
choiceExplanations: An exclusive one-cell assignment does not itself provide the shared-neuron structure described in the question. It is the strict local alternative.
Exactly identical activity patterns would fail to distinguish the concepts in that population. Shared contributors need not imply identical representations.
Forbidding shared contributors removes the overlap the question asks about. Sparse distributed coding can reuse neurons in different combinations.
Some shared contributors can support common features, while the nonshared contributors distinguish the concepts. This fits the review's sparse-coding rationale.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Review, slide 30; Study Guide: sparse representation, generalization, and categorization.

questions.prompt: In the Quiroga study question, what does 'invariant' refer to?
choices: An electrode never moving during a recording session.
A response that generalizes across different images depicting the same concept.
Every recorded neuron responding equally to every image category.
A participant giving exactly the same behavioral answer on every trial.
questions.explanation: The relevant invariance is representational: different visual examples of a concept can elicit a consistent selective response. It is not a claim about identical responses to all concepts.
choiceExplanations: Stable electrode placement is a recording consideration, but it is not what invariant representation means in the study's conceptual question.
The central test asks whether changing the visual example preserves the response associated with the same higher-level concept or identity.
Equal responses to all categories would remove the selectivity at issue. Invariance across examples of one concept is not indifference to concept identity.
The finding concerns neuronal firing across stimulus examples. Identical behavioral responses on every trial would not establish that neural invariance.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Review, slide 31; Study Guide: Quiroga methods and results.

questions.prompt: Which stimulus sampling strategy belongs to the reviewed Quiroga experiment?
choices: Presenting only voices of familiar and unfamiliar marmosets.
Presenting only repeated copies of one photograph of one person.
Presenting images from categories including faces, landmarks, objects, and animals.
Presenting only written descriptions of the patients' own brain lesions.
questions.explanation: The review describes varied visual images, including faces, landmarks, objects, and animals. This range helps assess selective responses rather than response to one repeatedly shown picture alone.
choiceExplanations: Voices and marmoset identity belong to the Tyree comparison. The reviewed Quiroga procedure emphasizes human patients viewing varied visual images.
Repeating one image alone would not test generalization across images or selectivity against varied alternatives. The reviewed stimulus set was broader.
These are the visual categories listed in the review. Their variety permits comparisons between preferred concepts and other tested images.
The review does not describe lesion narratives as stimuli. The study examines concept-related neuronal responses during visual image presentation.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Review, slide 31; Study Guide: Quiroga experimental methods.

questions.prompt: Which observation in the review argues against treating all of Quiroga's responsive neurons as strictly exclusive one-concept cells?
choices: A neuron responded consistently to different images depicting its preferred concept.
Some neurons responded to multiple tested stimuli rather than only one exclusive concept.
The recording method could resolve activity at the level of individual neurons.
Images were presented in a controlled order rather than selected spontaneously by patients.
questions.explanation: The review notes both selective invariant responses and responses to multiple stimuli. The coexistence of these observations fits a sparse-code interpretation better than strict universal exclusivity.
choiceExplanations: Invariance across examples is compatible with both a strict concept-selective unit and participation in a sparse code. It does not itself demonstrate nonexclusive preference.
Responses spanning multiple tested stimuli qualify the strict one-concept-only picture. Selective neurons can still contribute to sparse population codes.
Individual-neuron resolution reveals response preferences but does not determine whether each cell represents only one concept or participates in a population code.
Controlled presentation supports interpreting stimulus responses, but order alone does not establish whether the responsive neurons are exclusive to one concept.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Review, slide 31; Study Guide: implications of the Quiroga study.

questions.prompt: Which comparison is essential to Tyree's reviewed question about cross-modal identity?
choices: Whether a face shown at two visual sizes elicits a similar response.
Whether identity-selective responses occur in more than one animal species.
Whether different hippocampal neurons prefer different individual faces.
Whether information about an individual appears across that individual's face and voice presentations.
questions.explanation: Cross-modal identity concerns a common individual represented through different senses. Faces and voices provide the visual and auditory comparison emphasized in the review.
choiceExplanations: Changing size varies the visual example within one modality. It can test visual invariance, but it does not supply the face-versus-voice cross-modal comparison.
Cross-species generalization is a different question from cross-modal coding. Tyree's central comparison varies sensory presentations of individuals.
Different face preferences across neurons can reveal visual selectivity. Without voice responses, that observation does not establish generalization across modalities.
A face and a voice differ in sensory modality but can refer to the same individual. That relationship defines the reviewed cross-modal identity question.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Review, slide 32; Study Guide: Tyree cross-modal identity representation.

questions.prompt: The review reports cross-modal identity responses in a minority of sampled Tyree neurons. Which reading preserves the meaning of that finding?
choices: A subset of sampled neurons showed the described response; it was not a claim about every neuron.
Most tested animals could not recognize identities because most neurons did not meet this response criterion.
Each individual must occupy the same fixed fraction of all neurons in every primate brain.
The remaining neurons were proven incapable of contributing to any identity representation.
questions.explanation: The figure summarizes a subset of sampled neurons showing the specified response. It is not a behavioral score, a universal whole-brain proportion, or proof that other neurons contain no information.
choiceExplanations: This keeps the claim tied to the sampled cells and the response criterion in the review. It avoids turning a subset finding into a universal rule.
The fraction of cells meeting a response criterion is not the fraction of animals capable of recognition. Population activity may also contain identity information.
A result in sampled neurons does not establish a universal fixed allocation of cells to each identity throughout every primate brain.
Failure to meet this particular cross-modal response description does not establish that the remaining neurons contribute no identity-related information.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Review, slide 32; Study Guide: Tyree main results and implications.

questions.prompt: Which study-to-population mapping matches the course review?
choices: Quiroga: marmosets; Tyree: human epilepsy patients.
Quiroga: healthy infants; Tyree: human stroke patients.
Quiroga: human epilepsy patients; Tyree: marmosets.
Quiroga: human stroke patients; Tyree: healthy adult human volunteers.
questions.explanation: The review describes eight human epilepsy patients for Quiroga and four marmosets for Tyree. Keeping the populations separate helps interpret each study's access and generalizability.
choiceExplanations: This reverses the two study populations. The human implanted-electrode opportunity belongs to Quiroga, while the Tyree review describes marmosets.
Neither healthy infants nor human stroke patients are the study populations specified in these two reviewed concept-representation experiments.
This correctly assigns clinical human recordings to Quiroga and the marmoset identity study to Tyree, without conflating their participants.
The review does not describe either of these populations for the paired studies. Quiroga involved epilepsy patients and Tyree involved marmosets.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Review, slides 31–32; Study Guide: Quiroga and Tyree methods.

questions.prompt: Hypothetically, concept P activates neurons 2, 7, and 11; concept Q activates neurons 7, 12, and 19 in the same 200-neuron population. Which description best fits these patterns?
choices: Strict local coding, because each concept has its own exclusive single neuron.
Fully distributed coding, because neuron 7 participates in both patterns.
No representation, because the two concepts share a neuron.
Sparse coding, with a shared contributor and distinct overall subsets.
questions.explanation: Only a small part of the population responds for either concept. Shared neuron 7 does not erase the differences between the two activity patterns.
choiceExplanations: Each concept activates several neurons, and one contributor is shared. That is not the strict exclusive single-cell assignment specified here.
Sharing one neuron does not make a code fully distributed. Only three of the 200 neurons participate in each hypothetical pattern.
The patterns remain distinguishable because their other contributors differ. Overlap does not force the representations to be identical.
The small active fraction makes the code sparse, and the nonidentical combinations distinguish P from Q despite their shared contributor.
questions.sourceNote: Hypothetical application of PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Review, slides 29–30: sparse and distributed coding.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical neuron responds strongly to one photograph of a landmark but weakly to other photographs of that same landmark. What is the most important limitation of calling this an invariant landmark representation?
choices: The response does not generalize across the tested visual examples of the landmark.
The response should be called cross-modal invariance because several photographs were tested.
A strong response to one picture establishes a fully distributed representation throughout the population.
The response establishes exclusive landmark coding because one tested photograph was preferred.
questions.explanation: An invariant account requires generalization across changes in the visual example. Preference for one photograph can instead reflect features peculiar to that image.
choiceExplanations: Different photographs preserve the landmark's identity while changing its appearance. The inconsistent response therefore fails this tested invariance criterion.
Several photographs are still visual stimuli. This is variation within a modality, and the responses do not even generalize across those tested examples.
One cell's response to one image does not establish how broadly information is distributed across a population. The proposed population conclusion exceeds the evidence.
Image preference does not establish concept-level exclusivity. The weak response to other pictures of the same landmark makes an invariant identity interpretation uncertain.
questions.sourceNote: Hypothetical application of PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Review, slide 31: invariant visual representation.

questions.prompt: Hypothetically, a hippocampal neuron responds to every tested face and every tested voice, with no differences between individuals. Which description is best supported?
choices: It uniquely stores the identity of each tested individual.
It establishes that different individuals have no neural representations anywhere.
It responds across modalities, but these data do not show identity selectivity.
It demonstrates strict one-cell-per-person local coding.
questions.explanation: Cross-modal responsiveness alone is weaker than cross-modal identity coding. The latter requires information that distinguishes individuals while generalizing across their sensory presentations.
choiceExplanations: Equal responses to every individual do not establish a unique identity assignment. The measured response lacks the identity differences needed for that claim.
One unselective recorded response cannot rule out identity information in other cells or patterns. The inference must stay within the sampled data.
The neuron responds to both stimulus modalities, but its equal responses provide no tested distinction among identities. Modality breadth and identity selectivity differ.
Strict one-cell-per-person coding would require specificity to a particular individual, not the same response to every tested person and modality.
questions.sourceNote: Hypothetical application of PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Review, slide 32: cross-modal identity selectivity.

questions.prompt: A classmate says, 'Tyree found informative single neurons, so analyzing the population adds nothing.' Which reply best matches the review?
choices: Population activity matters only when every single neuron is completely silent.
The review reports identity information at both levels, so a selective cell does not exhaust the population's representation.
Population analyses reverse the study's species from marmosets to humans.
Analyzing many neurons automatically proves that every neuron is necessary for recognition.
questions.explanation: Tyree's reviewed findings include both cross-modal single-neuron responses and identity information in population activity. These levels can complement one another.
choiceExplanations: Population patterns are made from cellular activity, not universal silence. They can provide information even when some individual cells are selective.
The two analysis levels address complementary aspects of representation. A selective neuron can participate in a larger identity-related population pattern.
Changing the level of analysis does not change the study population. Both single-neuron and population evidence described here came from the marmoset study.
Recording information across neurons is not a necessity test. More recorded cells do not convert an observational response pattern into causal proof.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Review, slide 32; Study Guide: Tyree single-neuron and population results.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical population uses overlapping small subsets for familiar concepts. A newly learned concept is represented by a new combination of those contributors. Which argument from the review does this illustrate most directly?
choices: Learning requires a dedicated neuron that has never participated in any previous representation.
The new concept must be indistinguishable from old concepts because it reuses some of their neurons.
Sparse codes are only possible when every concept uses an entirely nonoverlapping subset.
Combinations of contributors can provide representational capacity and flexibility for new concepts.
questions.explanation: Recombining contributors can support additional representations without a strict one-new-concept/one-new-cell requirement. The review connects sparse coding with capacity, learning, and generalization.
choiceExplanations: That answer reinstates the strict dedicated-cell assumption. The hypothetical specifically represents the new concept through a combination of existing contributors.
Reuse does not require identical patterns. A new combination can differ from earlier combinations even when some contributing neurons are shared.
Nonoverlap is not required for sparse coding. Small subsets can overlap, allowing neurons to participate in different concept-related combinations.
Different combinations allow reuse without requiring identical concept patterns. This illustrates why sparse ensembles can support capacity and flexible learning.
questions.sourceNote: Hypothetical application of PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Review, slide 30: learning and sparse-representation advantages.

questions.prompt: A report of Quiroga's findings describes invariant responses in sampled medial temporal neurons, then concludes that every cortical region uses the same code. Where does the inference exceed the reviewed evidence?
choices: It extends findings from sampled neurons and recording regions to unexamined regions of the brain.
It interprets an invariant response as consistent with a higher-level concept rather than one exact image.
It recognizes that some neurons can respond to more than one tested stimulus.
It allows informative single neurons to participate in a broader sparse population code.
questions.explanation: The sampled cells and clinical recording locations constrain generalization. Evidence for a response pattern in those samples does not establish an identical code throughout all cortex.
choiceExplanations: This is the key scope error: a selective regional sample cannot establish a universal claim about unrecorded cortical areas and all their representations.
Generalization across images can support a higher-level interpretation, as in the reviewed finding. This does not create the unsupported whole-cortex extrapolation.
Responses to more than one tested stimulus are part of the review's description. Recognizing them appropriately qualifies strict exclusivity.
A selective cell can belong to a sparse population code. This compatibility is a cautious interpretation, unlike asserting the same code throughout all cortex.
questions.sourceNote: PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Review, slides 18 and 31; Study Guide: Quiroga implications and single-unit sampling limitations.

questions.prompt: Hypothetically, removing one contributor from a small ensemble leaves recognition possible, though less reliable. Which theory is most directly compatible with this pattern without adding a replacement cell?
choices: The removed cell was the unique and indispensable store of the concept.
Preserved recognition proves that the removed neuron never carried information about the concept.
Multiple contributors jointly carried the concept, leaving some representation after the loss.
Any decline in reliability rules out a distributed representation, which must be perfectly unaffected by cell loss.
questions.explanation: Surviving contributors can preserve information when one member is lost. This is the resilience argument for distributed representation; it need not predict perfectly unchanged performance.
choiceExplanations: If the cell were the sole indispensable store, its removal should not leave recognition supported by the same unchanged system. That is the strict account's fragility.
A contributor can carry information without being indispensable on its own. Other contributors may preserve performance after its removal.
An ensemble can retain partial information in its remaining members. Preserved but weaker performance is compatible with that distributed contribution.
Resilience need not mean zero effect. Losing one contributor can reduce available information while leaving enough in the remaining ensemble for imperfect recognition.
questions.sourceNote: Hypothetical application of PSYC 108 Midterm 1 Review, slide 30: neuron loss and sparse distributed representations.

questions.prompt: A proposed follow-up first changes the photograph while keeping identity fixed, then changes from face to voice while keeping identity fixed. How do these manipulations relate to the reviewed studies?
choices: Both manipulations test only whether a brain region is necessary after damage.
The first resembles visual invariance emphasized for Quiroga; the second resembles Tyree's cross-modal identity question.
The first is cross-modal because two photographs must use different senses.
The second eliminates identity information because a voice cannot refer to an individual.
questions.explanation: Both preserve identity while changing its presentation. Different photographs vary examples within vision; faces versus voices explicitly vary sensory modality.
choiceExplanations: Neither stimulus manipulation involves damage or disruption by itself. They address representational generalization rather than lesion-based necessity.
This accurately separates variation among visual examples from variation between visual and auditory presentations of a shared identity.
Two photographs remain visual stimuli even when their content differs. Cross-modal refers to a change in sensory modality, not just a new image.
